[Léo Delibes](./Léo_Delibes) and [Jules Massenet](./Jules_Massenet), among others.[[210]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMichelin2011-212) [Georges Bizet](./Georges_Bizet)'s [Carmen](./Carmen) premiered in 1875 and has become one of the most popular operas in the classical [canon](./Western_canon).[[229]](./Paris#cite_note-McClary-231)[[230]](./Paris#cite_note-232) Among the [Impressionist](./Impressionism_in_music) composers who created new works for piano, orchestra, opera, chamber music and other musical forms, stand in particular [Claude Debussy](./Claude_Debussy), [Erik Satie](./Erik_Satie) and [Maurice Ravel](./Maurice_Ravel). Several foreign-born composers, such as [Frédéric Chopin](./Frédéric_Chopin), [Franz Liszt](./Franz_Liszt), [Jacques Offenbach](./Jacques_Offenbach), [Niccolò Paganini](./Niccolò_Paganini), and [Igor Stravinsky](./Igor_Stravinsky), established themselves or made significant contributions both with their works and their influence in Paris.
[Bal-musette](./Bal-musette) is a style of French music and dance that first became popular in Paris in the 1870s; by 1880, Paris had some 150 dance halls.[[231]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDregni200419-233) Patrons danced the [bourrée](./Bourrée) to the accompaniment of the [cabrette](./Cabrette) (a [bellows](./Bellows)-blown [bagpipe](./Bagpipe) locally called a "musette") and the vielle à roue ([hurdy-gurdy](./Hurdy-gurdy)) in the cafés and bars of the city. Parisian and Italian musicians who played the [accordion](./Accordion) adopted the style and established themselves in Auvergnat bars,[[232]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDregni200832-234) and Paris became a major centre for [jazz](./Jazz) and still attracts jazz musicians from all around the world to its clubs and cafés.[[233]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMroue2006260-235) Paris is the spiritual home of [gypsy jazz](./Gypsy_jazz), and many of the Parisian jazzmen who developed in the first half of the 20th century began by playing Bal-musette in the city.[[232]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDregni200832-234) [Django Reinhardt](./Django_Reinhardt) rose to fame in Paris and performed with violinist [Stéphane Grappelli](./Stéphane_Grappelli) and their [Quintette du Hot Club de France](./Quintette_du_Hot_Club_de_France) in the 1930s and 1940s.[[234]](./Paris#cite_note-Gjazz-236)The [Moulin Rouge](./Moulin_Rouge) has hosted many singers including Parisian [Édith Piaf](./Édith_Piaf)
Immediately after the war, the [Saint-Germain-des-Prés](./Saint-Germain-des-Prés) quarter and the nearby Saint-Michel quarter became home to many small jazz clubs, including the Caveau des Lorientais, the Club Saint-Germain, the Rose Rouge, the Vieux-Colombier, and the most famous, [Le Tabou](./Le_Tabou). They introduced Parisians to the music of [Claude Luter](./Claude_Luter), [Boris Vian](./Boris_Vian), [Sydney Bechet](./Sydney_Bechet), [Mezz Mezzrow](./Mezz_Mezzrow), and [Henri Salvador](./Henri_Salvador). Most of the clubs closed by the early 1960s, as musical tastes shifted toward rock and roll.[[235]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBezbakh2004872-237)
Some of the finest [manouche](./Manouche) musicians in the world are found here playing the cafés of the city at night.[[234]](./Paris#cite_note-Gjazz-236) Some of the more notable jazz venues include the New Morning, Le Sunset, La Chope des Puces and Bouquet du Nord.[[233]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMroue2006260-235)[[234]](./Paris#cite_note-Gjazz-236) Several yearly festivals take place in Paris, including the [Paris Jazz Festival](./Paris_Jazz_Festival) and the rock festival [Rock en Seine](./Rock_en_Seine).[[236]](./Paris#cite_note-238) The [Orchestre de Paris](./Orchestre_de_Paris) was established in 1967.[[237]](./Paris#cite_note-andante-239) [Édith Piaf](./Édith_Piaf) is widely regarded as France's national [chanteuse](./Chanson) and one of France's greatest international stars.[[238]](./Paris#cite_note-yahoomusicbio-240)
Paris has a big [hip hop](./French_hip_hop) scene. This music became popular during the 1980s.[[239]](./Paris#cite_note-241)

### Cinema

See also: [List of films set in Paris](./List_of_films_set_in_Paris)Poster for the [Lumière brothers](./Auguste_and_Louis_Lumière) 1895 film [L'Arroseur Arrosé](./L'Arroseur_Arrosé), the earliest comedy, and the first film to portray a fictional story.
The movie industry was born in Paris when [Auguste and Louis Lumière](./Auguste_and_Louis_Lumière) projected the first motion picture for a paying audience at the Grand Café on 28 December 1895.[[240]](./Paris#cite_note-242) Many of Paris's concert/dance halls were transformed into cinemas when the media became popular beginning in the 1930s. Paris's largest cinema room today is in the [Grand Rex](./Grand_Rex) theatre with 2,700 seats.[[241]](./Paris#cite_note-243) Big multiplex cinemas have been built since the 1990s. UGC Ciné Cité Les Halles, with 27 screens, MK2 Bibliothèque with 20 screens, and UGC Ciné Cité Bercy with 18 screens are among the largest.[[242]](./Paris#cite_note-244)
Parisians tend to share the same movie-going trends as many of the world's global cities, with cinemas primarily dominated by Hollywood-generated film entertainment. [French cinema](./Cinema_of_France) comes a close second, with major directors (réalisateurs) such as [Claude Lelouch](./Claude_Lelouch), [Jean-Luc Godard](./Jean-Luc_Godard), and [Luc Besson](./Luc_Besson), and the more slapstick/popular genre with director [Claude Zidi](./Claude_Zidi) as an example.[[243]](./Paris#cite_note-245)

### Restaurants and cuisine

See also: [French cuisine](./French_cuisine)Le Zimmer, on the [Place du Châtelet](./Place_du_Châtelet)
Since the late 18th century, Paris has been famous for its restaurants and [haute cuisine](./Haute_cuisine), food meticulously prepared and artfully presented. La Taverne Anglaise, opened in 1786 in the arcades of the [Palais-Royal](./Palais-Royal) by [Antoine Beauvilliers](./Antoine_Beauvilliers); it became a model for future luxury Paris restaurants. The restaurant [Le Grand Véfour](./Le_Grand_Véfour) in the Palais-Royal dates from the same period.[[244]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro19961136–1138-246) The famous Paris restaurants of the 19th century, including the Café de Paris, the [Rocher de Cancale](./Au_Rocher_de_Cancale), the [Café Anglais](./Café_Anglais), [Maison Dorée](./Maison_dorée_(Paris)) and the Café Riche, were mostly located near the theatres on the [Boulevard des Italiens](./Boulevard_des_Italiens). Several of the best-known restaurants in Paris today appeared during the [Belle Époque](./Belle_Époque), including [Maxim's](./Maxim's_Paris) on Rue Royale, [Ledoyen](./Ledoyen) in the gardens of the [Champs-Élysées](./Champs-Élysées), and the [Tour d'Argent](./Tour_d'Argent) on the Quai de la Tournelle.[[245]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro19961137-247)
Today, owing to Paris's cosmopolitan population, every French regional cuisine and almost every national cuisine in the world can be found there; the city has more than 9,000 restaurants.[[246]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDominé2014-248) The [Michelin Guide](./Michelin_Guide) has been a standard guide to French restaurants since 1900, awarding its highest award, three stars, to the best restaurants in France. In 2018, of the 27 Michelin three-star restaurants in France, ten are located in Paris. These include both restaurants that serve classical French cuisine, such as [L'Ambroisie](./L'Ambroisie), and those that serve non-traditional menus, such as [L'Astrance](./L'Astrance), which combines French and Asian cuisines. Several of France's most famous chefs, including [Pierre Gagnaire](./Pierre_Gagnaire), [Alain Ducasse](./Alain_Ducasse), [Yannick Alléno](./Yannick_Alléno), and [Alain Passard](./Alain_Passard), have three-star restaurants in Paris.[[247]](./Paris#cite_note-249)[[248]](./Paris#cite_note-250)[Les Deux Magots](./Les_Deux_Magots) café on Boulevard Saint-Germain
Paris has several other kinds of traditional eating places. The [café](./Coffeehouse) arrived in Paris in the 17th century, and by the 18th century, Parisian cafés were centres of the city's political and cultural life. The [Café Procope](./Café_Procope) on the Left Bank dates from this period. In the 20th century, the cafés of the Left Bank, especially [Café de la Rotonde](./Café_de_la_Rotonde) and [Le Dôme Café](./Le_Dôme_Café) in Montparnasse and [Café de Flore](./Café_de_Flore) and [Les Deux Magots](./Les_Deux_Magots) on Boulevard Saint Germain, all still in business, were important meeting places for painters, writers and philosophers.[[245]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro19961137-247) A [bistro](./Bistro) is a type of eating place loosely defined as a neighbourhood restaurant with a modest decor and prices and a regular clientele, and a congenial atmosphere. Real bistros are increasingly rare in Paris, due to rising costs, competition, and different eating habits of Parisian diners.[[249]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996715-251) A [brasserie](./Brasserie) originally was a tavern located next to a brewery, which served beer and food at any hour. Beginning with the [Paris Exposition of 1867](./Paris_Exposition_of_1867), it became a popular kind of restaurant which featured beer and other beverages served by young women in the national costume associated with the beverage. Now, brasseries, like cafés, serve food and drinks throughout the day.[[250]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996773-252)

### Fashion

Main article: [Fashion in Paris](./Fashion_in_Paris)[Magdalena Frackowiak](./Magdalena_Frackowiak) at [Paris Fashion Week](./Paris_Fashion_Week) (Autumn 2011)
Since the 19th century, Paris has been an international [fashion capital](./Fashion_capital), particularly in the domain of [haute couture](./Haute_couture) (clothing hand-made to order for private clients).[[251]](./Paris#cite_note-253) It is home to some of the largest fashion houses in the world, including [Dior](./Christian_Dior_S.A.) and [Chanel](./Chanel), as well as many other well-known and more contemporary fashion designers, such as [Karl Lagerfeld](./Karl_Lagerfeld), [Jean-Paul Gaultier](./Jean-Paul_Gaultier), [Yves Saint Laurent](./Yves_Saint_Laurent_(designer)), [Givenchy](./Givenchy), and [Christian Lacroix](./Christian_Lacroix). [Paris Fashion Week](./Paris_Fashion_Week), held in January and July in the [Carrousel du Louvre](./Carrousel_du_Louvre) among other renowned city locations, is one of the top four events on the international fashion calendar.[[252]](./Paris#cite_note-254)[[253]](./Paris#cite_note-255) Moreover, Paris is also the home of the world's largest [cosmetics](./Cosmetics) company, [L'Oréal](./L'Oréal), as well as three of the top five global makers of luxury fashion accessories: [Louis Vuitton](./Louis_Vuitton), [Hermés](./Hermés), and [Cartier](./Cartier_(jeweler)).[[254]](./Paris#cite_note-256) Most of the major fashion designers have their showrooms along the [Avenue Montaigne](./Avenue_Montaigne), between the [Champs-Élysées](./Champs-Élysées) and the Seine.

### Photography

The inventor [Nicéphore Niépce](./Nicéphore_Niépce) produced the first permanent photograph on a polished pewter plate in Paris in 1825. In 1839, [Louis Daguerre](./Louis_Daguerre) patented the [Daguerrotype](./Daguerrotype), which became the most common form of photography until the 1860s.[[210]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMichelin2011-212) The work of [Étienne-Jules Marey](./Étienne-Jules_Marey) in the 1880s contributed considerably to the development of modern photography. Photography came to occupy a central role in Parisian Surrealist activity, in the works of [Man Ray](./Man_Ray) and [Maurice Tabard](./Maurice_Tabard).[[255]](./Paris#cite_note-257)[[256]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHazan2011362-258) Numerous photographers achieved renown for their photography of Paris, including [Eugène Atget](./Eugène_Atget), noted for his depictions of street scenes; [Robert Doisneau](./Robert_Doisneau), noted for his playful pictures of people and market scenes (among which Le baiser de l'hôtel de ville has become iconic of the romantic vision of Paris); [Marcel Bovis](./Marcel_Bovis), noted for his night scenes; [Jacques-Henri Lartigue](./Jacques-Henri_Lartigue); and [Henri Cartier-Bresson](./Henri_Cartier-Bresson).[[210]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMichelin2011-212) [Poster art](./Poster_art) also became an important art form in Paris in the late nineteenth century, through the work of [Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](./Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec), [Jules Chéret](./Jules_Chéret), [Eugène Grasset](./Eugène_Grasset), [Adolphe Willette](./Adolphe_Willette), [Pierre Bonnard](./Pierre_Bonnard), [Georges de Feure](./Georges_de_Feure), [Henri-Gabriel Ibels](./Henri-Gabriel_Ibels), [Paul Gavarni](./Paul_Gavarni) and [Alphonse Mucha](./Alphonse_Mucha).[[210]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMichelin2011-212)

### Media
Founded in 1826, [Le Figaro](./Le_Figaro) is still considered a [newspaper of record](./Newspaper_of_record).[[257]](./Paris#cite_note-259)
Paris and its close suburbs are home to numerous newspapers, magazines and publications including [Le Monde](./Le_Monde), [Le Figaro](./Le_Figaro), [Libération](./Libération), [Le Nouvel Observateur](./Le_Nouvel_Observateur), [Le Canard enchaîné](./Le_Canard_enchaîné), [La Croix](./La_Croix_(newspaper)), [Le Parisien](./Le_Parisien) (in [Saint-Ouen](./Saint-Ouen,_Seine-Saint-Denis)), [Les Échos](./Les_Échos_(France)), Paris Match ([Neuilly-sur-Seine](./Neuilly-sur-Seine)), Réseaux & Télécoms, [Reuters](./Reuters) France, [l'Équipe](./L'Équipe) ([Boulogne-Billancourt](./Boulogne-Billancourt)) and L'Officiel des Spectacles.[[258]](./Paris#cite_note-260) France's two most prestigious newspapers, Le Monde and Le Figaro, are the centrepieces of the Parisian publishing industry.[[259]](./Paris#cite_note-261) [Agence France-Presse](./Agence_France-Presse) is France's oldest continually operating news agency and is headquartered in Paris.[[260]](./Paris#cite_note-262) [France 24](./France_24) is a television news channel owned and operated by the French government.[[261]](./Paris#cite_note-263) France Diplomatie, owned and operated by the [Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs](./Ministry_of_Foreign_and_European_Affairs_(France)), pertains solely to diplomatic news and occurrences.[[262]](./Paris#cite_note-264)
The most-viewed network in France, [TF1](./TF1), is in nearby [Boulogne-Billancourt](./Boulogne-Billancourt). [France 2](./France_2), [France 3](./France_3), [Canal+](./Canal+_(French_TV_channel)), [France 5](./France_5), [M6](./M6_(TV_channel)) ([Neuilly-sur-Seine](./Neuilly-sur-Seine)), [Arte](./Arte), [D8](./D8_(TV_channel)), [W9](./W9_(TV_channel)), [NT1](./NT1_(TV_channel)), [NRJ 12](./NRJ_12), [La Chaîne parlementaire](./La_Chaîne_parlementaire), [France 4](./France_4), [BFM TV](./BFM_TV), and [Gulli](./Gulli) are other stations located in and around the capital.[[263]](./Paris#cite_note-265) [Radio France](./Radio_France), France's public radio broadcaster, and its various channels, is headquartered in Paris's [16th arrondissement](./16th_arrondissement_of_Paris). [Radio France Internationale](./Radio_France_Internationale), another public broadcaster, is also based in the city.[[264]](./Paris#cite_note-266) Paris also holds the headquarters of the [La Poste](./La_Poste_(France)), France's national postal carrier.[[265]](./Paris#cite_note-267)

### Holidays and festivals

[Bastille Day](./Bastille_Day), a celebration of the storming of the Bastille in 1789, the biggest festival in the city, is a military parade taking place every year on 14 July on the [Champs-Élysées](./Champs-Élysées), from the [Arc de Triomphe](./Arc_de_Triomphe) to [Place de la Concorde](./Place_de_la_Concorde). It includes a [flypast](./Flypast) over the Champs Élysées by the [Patrouille de France](./Patrouille_de_France), a parade of military units and equipment, and a display of fireworks in the evening, the most spectacular being the one at the Eiffel Tower.[[266]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackmoreMcConnachie2004204-268)
Other yearly festivals include [Paris-Plages](./Paris-Plages), a festive summertime event when the Right Bank of the Seine is converted into a temporary beach;[[266]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlackmoreMcConnachie2004204-268) [Journées du Patrimoine](./European_Heritage_Days), [Fête de la Musique](./Fête_de_la_Musique), Techno Parade, [Nuit Blanche](./Nuit_Blanche), Cinéma au clair de lune, Printemps des rues, Festival d'automne, and Fête des jardins. The [Carnaval de Paris](./Paris_Carnival), one of the oldest festivals in Paris, dates back to the Middle Ages.

### Libraries

Main article: [Libraries in Paris](./Libraries_in_Paris)
The [Bibliothèque nationale de France](./Bibliothèque_nationale_de_France) (BnF) operates public libraries in Paris, among them the François Mitterrand Library, Richelieu Library, Louvois, Opéra Library, and [Arsenal Library](./Bibliothèque_de_l'Arsenal).[[267]](./Paris#cite_note-269)[Sainte-Geneviève Library](./Sainte-Geneviève_Library)
The [Bibliothèque Forney](./Bibliothèque_Forney), in the Marais district, is dedicated to the decorative arts; the Arsenal Library occupies a former military building, and has a large collection on French literature; and the [Bibliothèque historique de la ville de Paris](./Bibliothèque_historique_de_la_ville_de_Paris), also in Le Marais, contains the Paris historical research service. The [Sainte-Geneviève Library](./Sainte-Geneviève_Library), designed by [Henri Labrouste](./Henri_Labrouste) and built in the mid-1800s, contains a rare book and manuscript division.[[268]](./Paris#cite_note-Woodward2006-270) [Bibliothèque Mazarine](./Bibliothèque_Mazarine) is the oldest public library in France. The [Médiathèque Musicale Mahler](./Médiathèque_Musicale_Mahler) opened in 1986 and contains collections related to music. The François Mitterrand Library (nicknamed Très Grande Bibliothèque) was completed in 1994 to a design of [Dominique Perrault](./Dominique_Perrault) and contains four glass towers.[[268]](./Paris#cite_note-Woodward2006-270)
There are several academic libraries and archives in Paris. The [Sorbonne Library](./Bibliothèque_de_la_Sorbonne) is the largest university library in Paris. In addition to the [Sorbonne](./Sorbonne_(building)) location, there are branches in Malesherbes, Clignancourt-Championnet, Michelet-[Institut d'Art et d'Archéologie](./Institut_d'Art_et_d'Archéologie), Serpente-Maison de la Recherche, and Institut des Etudes Ibériques.[[269]](./Paris#cite_note-271) Other academic libraries include Interuniversity Pharmaceutical Library, Leonardo da Vinci University Library, Paris School of Mines Library, and the René Descartes University Library.[[270]](./Paris#cite_note-nd.edu-272)

##  Sports

See also: [Football in Paris](./Football_in_Paris)[Parc des Princes](./Parc_des_Princes), the stadium of Paris Saint-Germain
Paris's major sports clubs are the [association football](./Association_football) club [Paris Saint-Germain F.C.](./Paris_Saint-Germain_F.C.) (PSG)[[271]](./Paris#cite_note-273) and the [rugby union](./Rugby_union) clubs [Stade Français](./Stade_Français) and [Racing 92](./Racing_92).[[272]](./Paris#cite_note-274) The 80,000-seat [Stade de France](./Stade_de_France), built for the [1998 FIFA World Cup](./1998_FIFA_World_Cup), is located just north of Paris in the commune of [Saint-Denis](./Saint-Denis,_Seine-Saint-Denis).[[273]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand2010300–301-275) It is used for football, rugby union, and track and field athletics. It hosts the [France national football team](./France_national_football_team) for friendlies and major tournaments qualifiers, the [French national rugby team](./France_national_rugby_union_team)'s home matches of the [Six Nations Championship](./Six_Nations_Championship), and several important matches of the Stade Français rugby team.[[273]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand2010300–301-275) The city and closer suburbs have several other professional and amateur football clubs, including [Paris FC](./Paris_FC) and [Red Star FC](./Red_Star_FC).[[274]](./Paris#cite_note-276)[[275]](./Paris#cite_note-277)
[Rugby league](./Rugby_league) is not as popular in Paris as in other areas of France. Despite this, the capital has hosted several major events in the sport's history since the country's first game, an exhibition match between the [Australia national team](./Australia_national_rugby_league_team) and a [British League](./Rugby_Football_League) Select XIII, in December 1933. The [Rugby League World Cup](./Rugby_League_World_Cup) was first held in [1954](./1954_Rugby_League_World_Cup) with the [Parc des Princes](./Parc_des_Princes#Second_stadium_(1932–1972)) hosting the opening match and the [final](./1954_Rugby_League_World_Cup_final) in which [France](./France_national_rugby_league_team) finished as runners-up to [Great Britain](./Great_Britain_national_rugby_league_team). The newly rebuilt [Parc des Princes](./Parc_des_Princes) was later used for a group game of the [1972 Rugby League World Cup](./1972_Rugby_League_World_Cup). A [rugby league department](./Paris_Saint-Germain_Rugby_League) of PSG was created to participate in the [Super League](./Super_League).[[276]](./Paris#cite_note-278) In 2006, [Catalans Dragons](./Catalans_Dragons) became the first French side to enter the [British rugby league system](./British_rugby_league_system) following PSG's withdrawal.[[277]](./Paris#cite_note-279)
Paris was the first city to host the [Summer Olympics](./Summer_Olympic_Games) twice and the second to host three times, hosting in [1900](./1900_Summer_Olympics), [1924](./1924_Summer_Olympics) and [2024](./2024_Summer_Olympics).[[278]](./Paris#cite_note-280) The city also hosted the finals of the [1938 FIFA World Cup](./1938_FIFA_World_Cup_final), [1998 FIFA World Cup](./1998_FIFA_World_Cup_final), [2007 Rugby World Cup](./2007_Rugby_World_Cup_Final) and [2023 Rugby World Cup](./2023_Rugby_World_Cup_final), at the Stade de France. Paris hosted the finals of the [1960](./1960_European_Nations'_Cup_final), [1984](./UEFA_Euro_1984_final) and [2016](./UEFA_Euro_2016_final) UEFA European Championships.[[279]](./Paris#cite_note-281) Paris held six [UEFA Champions League](./UEFA_Champions_League) finals, including the [2022](./2022_UEFA_Champions_League_Final) edition.[[280]](./Paris#cite_note-282)2010 Tour de France, [Champs Élysées](./Champs_Élysées)
The final stage of the [Tour de France](./Tour_de_France) finishes in Paris; since 1975, the race has [finished on the Champs-Elysées](./Champs-Élysées_stage_in_the_Tour_de_France).[[281]](./Paris#cite_note-283) Two annual [tennis](./Tennis) tournaments are held in Paris: the [French Open](./French_Open), held every year on the [red clay](./Red_clay) of the [Stade Roland Garros](./Stade_Roland_Garros),[[282]](./Paris#cite_note-284) one of the four [Grand Slam](./Grand_Slam_(tennis)) events of the world professional tennis tour, and the [Paris Masters](./Paris_Masters), held in the [Bercy Arena](./AccorHotels_Arena).[[283]](./Paris#cite_note-285)
[Basketball](./Basketball) teams [Levallois SCB](./Levallois_Sporting_Club_Basket) and [Paris Basket Racing](./Paris_Basket_Racing) merged in 2007 to create club [Metropolitans 92](./Metropolitans_92), which plays some of its games at the [Stade Pierre de Coubertin](./Stade_Pierre_de_Coubertin_(Paris)).[[284]](./Paris#cite_note-286) Paris also features [Paris Basketball](./Paris_Basketball) in Basketball,[[285]](./Paris#cite_note-287) [Paris Saint-Germain](./Paris_Saint-Germain_Handball) in [handball](./Handball)[[286]](./Paris#cite_note-288) and [Paris Musketeers](./Paris_Musketeers) in [American football](./American_football).[[287]](./Paris#cite_note-289)

##  Infrastructure

### Transport

Main article: [Transport in Paris](./Transport_in_Paris)The [Gare du Nord](./Gare_du_Nord) railway station is the busiest in Europe.
Paris is a major rail, highway, and air transport hub. The [Île-de-France Mobilités](./Île-de-France_Mobilités) (IDFM) oversees the transit network in the region.[[288]](./Paris#cite_note-stif-290) The syndicate coordinates public transport. The [RATP](./RATP_Group) operates 347 [bus](./Bus_(RATP)) lines, the [Métro](./Paris_Métro), eight tramway lines, and sections of the RER. The [SNCF](./SNCF) operates suburban rails, one tramway line, and other sections of the RER. The [Optile](./Optile) consortium of private operators manages 1,176 bus lines.[[289]](./Paris#cite_note-291)
Paris has one of the most [sustainable](./Sustainable_transport) transportation systems in the world[[6]](./Paris#cite_note-ICLEI-7)[[290]](./Paris#cite_note-292) and is one of only two cities that received the [Sustainable Transport Award](./Sustainable_Transport_Award) twice, in 2008 and 2023.[[291]](./Paris#cite_note-Award-293) In 2022–2023, 53.3% of trips in Paris were made on foot, 30% on public transport, 11.2% on bicycles and 4.3% on cars.[[292]](./Paris#cite_note-294)[[293]](./Paris#cite_note-295) Paris has banned the most polluting automobiles from key districts[[294]](./Paris#cite_note-296)[[295]](./Paris#cite_note-297) and is doubling bike lanes. The concept of the [15-minute city](./15-minute_city) was created by [Carlos Moreno](./Carlos_Moreno_(urbanist)), a professor from Paris, and began to be implemented by its mayor [Anne Hidalgo](./Anne_Hidalgo).[[296]](./Paris#cite_note-298)

#### Walking

Paris is a highly [walkable](./Walkable) city and tries to increase its mode share beyond[[297]](./Paris#cite_note-299)[[298]](./Paris#cite_note-300) 53% of all trips in 2024.[[299]](./Paris#cite_note-301) The number of trips made by foot in the Grand Paris metropolis increased by 50% from 2000 to 2018.[[300]](./Paris#cite_note-302)

#### Railways

See also: [List of Paris railway stations](./List_of_Paris_railway_stations)
Main articles: [Paris Métro](./Paris_Métro), [Réseau Express Régional](./Réseau_Express_Régional), [Transilien](./Transilien), and [Tramways in Île-de-France](./Tramways_in_Île-de-France)The [Paris Métro](./Paris_Métro) is the busiest subway network in the European Union.
A central hub of the national rail network, Paris's six major railway stations ([Gare du Nord](./Gare_du_Nord), [Gare de l'Est](./Gare_de_l'Est), [Gare de Lyon](./Gare_de_Lyon), [Gare d'Austerlitz](./Gare_d'Austerlitz), [Gare Montparnasse](./Gare_Montparnasse), [Gare Saint-Lazare](./Gare_Saint-Lazare)) and a minor one ([Gare de Bercy](./Gare_de_Bercy)) are connected to three networks: [high-speed rail](./High-speed_rail) lines ([TGV](./TGV), [Eurostar](./Eurostar), [Intercity Express](./Intercity_Express), [Frecciarossa](./Frecciarossa)), normal speed trains ([Intercités](./Intercités), [Intercités de nuit](./Intercités_de_nuit), [Nightjet](./Nightjet), [TER](./Transport_express_régional)), and the suburban rails ([Transilien](./Transilien)). The Transilien is the [commuter rail](./Commuter_rail) network serving [Paris region](./Île-de-France), through 9 lines, 392 stations and 1,294 km (804.1 mi) of rails.
Since the inauguration of its first line in 1900, Paris's Métro network has grown to become the city's most widely used local transport system. In 2015, it carried about 5.23 million passengers daily.[[301]](./Paris#cite_note-303) There are 16 lines, 321 stations (405 stops) and 245.6 km (152.6 mi) of rails. Superimposed on this is a [regional express network](./Réseau_Express_Régional), the RER, whose five lines, 257 stops, and 602 km (374 mi) of rails connect Paris to more distant parts of the urban area. With over 1.4 million passengers per day, [RER A](./RER_A) is the busiest metro line in Europe. The [Paris region](./Île-de-France) is served by [a light rail network, the tramway](./Tramways_in_Île-de-France). Opened in 1992, fifteen lines are now operational, spanning 196.6 kilometres (122.2 mi) with 283 stations.

#### Air
In 2023, [Charles de Gaulle Airport](./Charles_de_Gaulle_Airport) was the third-busiest airport in Europe and the eleventh-busiest airport in the world.[[302]](./Paris#cite_note-304)
Paris is served by three commercial international airports: [Charles de Gaulle Airport](./Charles_de_Gaulle_Airport), the [third-busiest airport in Europe](./List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe) as of 2018[[update]](//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paris&action=edit),[[303]](./Paris#cite_note-305)[[304]](./Paris#cite_note-306) [Orly Airport](./Orly_Airport) and [Beauvais–Tillé Airport](./Beauvais–Tillé_Airport). In 2019, these three airports recorded traffic of 112 million passengers,[[305]](./Paris#cite_note-307) making them the [5th busiest airport system in the world](./World's_busiest_city_airport_systems_by_passenger_traffic). There is also one [general aviation](./General_aviation) airport, [Paris–Le Bourget Airport](./Paris–Le_Bourget_Airport), historically the oldest Parisian airport and closest to the city centre, which is now used only for private business flights and air shows. Charles de Gaulle Airport, located on the edge of the northern suburbs of Paris, opened to commercial traffic in 1974 and became the busiest Parisian airport in 1993.[[306]](./Paris#cite_note-308) In 2023, it was the [4th busiest airport in the world by international traffic](./List_of_busiest_airports_by_international_passenger_traffic) and it is the hub for the nation's [flag carrier](./Flag_carrier), [Air France](./Air_France).[[307]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand2010278–283-309) Beauvais-Tillé Airport, located 69 km (43 mi) north of Paris's city centre, is used by charter airlines and [low-cost carriers](./Low-cost_carriers).

#### Motorways
The [Boulevard Périphérique](./Boulevard_Périphérique)
Paris is the most important hub of France's [motorway](./Motorway) network, and is surrounded by three orbital freeways: the [Périphérique](./Périphérique_(Paris)),[[91]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201069-93) which follows the approximate path of 19th-century fortifications around Paris, the [A86](./A86_autoroute) motorway in the inner suburbs, and the [Francilienne](./Francilienne) motorway in the outer suburbs. Paris has an extensive road network with over 2,000 km (1,243 mi) of highways and motorways.

#### Waterways

The Paris region is the most active water transport area in France. Most of the cargo is handled by the [Ports of Paris](./Autonomous_Port_of_Paris), in facilities located around Paris. The rivers [Loire](./Loire), [Rhine](./Rhine), [Rhône](./Rhône), [Meuse](./Meuse), and [Scheldt](./Scheldt) can be reached by canals connecting with the Seine, which include the [Canal Saint-Martin](./Canal_Saint-Martin), [Canal Saint-Denis](./Canal_Saint-Denis), and the Canal de l'Ourcq.[[308]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJefferson2009114-310)

#### Cycling
[Vélib'](./Vélib') at the [Place de la Bastille](./Place_de_la_Bastille)
There are 440 km (270 mi) of [cycle paths and routes in Paris](./Cycling_in_Paris). These include piste cyclable, bike lanes separated from other traffic by physical barriers, and bande cyclable, a bicycle lane denoted by a painted path on the road). Some 29 km (18 mi) of specially marked bus lanes are free for use by cyclists, with a protective barrier against encroachments from vehicles.[[309]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHart2004355-311) Cyclists have the right to ride in both directions on certain one-way streets. Paris has a [bike sharing](./Community_bicycle_program) system called [Vélib'](./Vélib') with more than 20,000 public bicycles distributed at 1,800 parking stations.[[310]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTERand2010165-312)

### Electricity

See also: [Electricity sector in France](./Electricity_sector_in_France)
In 2012, around 50% of electricity generated in the [Île-de-France](./Île-de-France) came from cogeneration energy plants. Other energy sources included thermal power (35%), waste incineration (9% – with cogeneration plants, these provide the city with heat as well), methane gas (5%), hydraulics (1%), and solar power (0.1%).[[311]](./Paris#cite_note-prod_electrique_IDF-313) A quarter of the city's [district heating](./District_heating) is to come from a plant in [Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine](./Saint-Ouen-sur-Seine), burning a 50/50-mix of coal and [wood pellets](./Wood_pellets).[[312]](./Paris#cite_note-314)

### Water and sanitation
The Seine, the [Île de la Cité](./Île_de_la_Cité) and a [Bateau Mouche](./Bateau_Mouche)
Paris in its early history had only the rivers Seine and [Bièvre](./Bièvre_(river)) for water. From 1809, the [Canal de l'Ourcq](./Canal_de_l'Ourcq) provided Paris with water from less-polluted rivers to the north-east of the capital.[[313]](./Paris#cite_note-315) From 1857, the civil engineer [Eugène Belgrand](./Eugène_Belgrand), under [Napoleon III](./Napoleon_III), oversaw the construction of a series of new aqueducts that brought water from locations all around the city to several reservoirs.[[314]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurchell197193-316)
From then on, the new reservoir system became Paris's principal source of drinking water. The remains of the old system, pumped into lower levels of the same reservoirs, were from then on used for the cleaning of Paris's streets. This system is still a major part of Paris's water-supply network. Today, Paris has more than 2,400 km (1,491 mi) of underground sewers.[[315]](./Paris#cite_note-sewers-317)
[Air pollution](./Air_pollution) in Paris, from the point of view of [particulate matter](./Particulates) (PM10), is the highest in France with 38 μg/m3.[[316]](./Paris#cite_note-318) Paris has one of the highest levels of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the EU.[[317]](./Paris#cite_note-319)

### Parks and gardens

Main articles: [List of parks and gardens in Paris](./List_of_parks_and_gardens_in_Paris) and [History of Parks and Gardens of Paris](./History_of_Parks_and_Gardens_of_Paris)The lawns of the [Parc des Buttes-Chaumont](./Parc_des_Buttes-Chaumont) on a sunny day
Paris has more than 421 municipal parks and gardens, covering more than 3,000 hectares and containing more than 250,000 trees.[[318]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJarrassé20076-320) Two of Paris's oldest and most famous gardens are the [Tuileries Garden](./Tuileries_Garden), created in 1564 for the [Tuileries Palace](./Tuileries_Palace) and redone by [André Le Nôtre](./André_Le_Nôtre) between 1664 and 1672,[[319]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand2010125-321) and the [Luxembourg Garden](./Luxembourg_Garden), for the [Luxembourg Palace](./Luxembourg_Palace), built for [Marie de' Medici](./Marie_de'_Medici) in 1612, which today houses the [Senate](./Senate_(France)).[[320]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand2010208-322) The [Jardin des plantes](./Jardin_des_plantes) was the first botanical garden in Paris, created in 1626.[[321]](./Paris#cite_note-323)
Between 1853 and 1870, Emperor [Napoleon III](./Napoleon_III) and the city's first director of parks and gardens, [Jean-Charles Adolphe Alphand](./Jean-Charles_Adolphe_Alphand), created the [Bois de Boulogne](./Bois_de_Boulogne), [Bois de Vincennes](./Bois_de_Vincennes), [Parc Montsouris](./Parc_Montsouris) and [Parc des Buttes-Chaumont](./Parc_des_Buttes-Chaumont), located at the four compass points around Paris, as well as many smaller parks, squares and gardens in the Paris's quarters.[[322]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJarrassé2007122–161-324) Since 1977, the city has created 166 new parks, most notably the [Parc de la Villette](./Parc_de_la_Villette) (1987), [Parc André Citroën](./Parc_André_Citroën) (1992), [Parc de Bercy](./Parc_de_Bercy) (1997) and [Parc Clichy-Batignolles](./Parc_Clichy-Batignolles_–_Martin-Luther-King) (2007).[[323]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJarrassé2007242–256-325) One of the newest parks, the [Promenade des Berges de la Seine](./Promenade_des_Berges_de_la_Seine) (2013), has floating gardens.

### Cemeteries
The [Paris Catacombs](./Catacombs_of_Paris) hold the remains of approximately 6 million people.
During the Roman era, Paris's main cemetery was located on the outskirts of the [left bank](./Rive_Gauche) settlement. This changed with the rise of Catholic Christianity, where almost every inner-city church had adjoining burial grounds for use by their parishes. With Paris's growth, many of these, particularly the city's largest cemetery, the [Holy Innocents' Cemetery](./Holy_Innocents'_Cemetery), were filled to overflowing. When inner-city burials were condemned from 1786, the contents of all Paris's parish cemeteries were transferred to a renovated section of [Paris's stone mines](./Mines_of_Paris), today [place Denfert-Rochereau](./Place_Denfert-Rochereau) in the 14th arrondissement.[[324]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhaley2012101-326)[[325]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBroadwell200792-327)
After a tentative creation of several smaller suburban cemeteries, the Prefect Nicholas Frochot under [Napoleon](./Napoleon) Bonaparte provided a more definitive solution in the creation of three massive Parisian cemeteries outside the city limits.[[326]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAyers2004271-328) Open from 1804, these were the cemeteries of [Père Lachaise](./Père_Lachaise_Cemetery), [Montmartre](./Montmartre_Cemetery), [Montparnasse](./Montparnasse_Cemetery), and later [Passy](./Passy_Cemetery). New suburban cemeteries were created in the early 20th century: The largest of these are the [Cimetière parisien de Saint-Ouen](./Saint-Ouen_Cemetery), the [Cimetière parisien de Pantin](./Cimetière_parisien_de_Pantin), also known as Cimetière parisien de [Pantin](./Pantin)-[Bobigny](./Bobigny), the Cimetière parisien d'[Ivry](./Ivry-sur-Seine), and the Cimetière parisien de [Bagneux](./Bagneux,_Hauts-de-Seine).[[327]](./Paris#cite_note-Parisian_Cemeteries-329) Famous people buried in Parisian cemeteries include [Oscar Wilde](./Oscar_Wilde), [Frédéric Chopin](./Frédéric_Chopin), [Jim Morrison](./Jim_Morrison), [Édith Piaf](./Édith_Piaf) and [Serge Gainsbourg](./Serge_Gainsbourg).[[328]](./Paris#cite_note-330)

### Education

Main article: [Education in Paris](./Education_in_Paris)The [Sorbonne University](./Sorbonne_University)
In 2009, around 40 percent of Parisians held a [licence](./Licence_(France))-level diploma or higher, the highest proportion in France.[[329]](./Paris#cite_note-331) 13 percent have no diploma, the third-lowest percentage in France. Education in Paris and the Île-de-France region employs approximately 330,000 people, 170,000 of whom are teachers and professors, teaching approximately 2.9 million students in around 9,000 primary, secondary, and higher education schools and institutions.[[330]](./Paris#cite_note-idf_education-332)
The [University of Paris](./University_of_Paris), founded in the 12th century, is often called the [Sorbonne](./University_of_Paris) after one of its original medieval colleges. In 1970, it was broken up into [thirteen autonomous universities](./List_of_universities_and_institutions_in_the_Paris_region) following the [student demonstrations in 1968](./May_68). Most of the campuses today are in the [Latin Quarter](./Latin_Quarter,_Paris), where the old university was located, while others are scattered around the city and the suburbs.[[331]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTECombeau2013213–214-333)
The Paris region hosts France's highest concentration of the [grandes écoles](./Grandes_écoles) – 55 specialised centres of higher education outside or inside the public university structure. The prestigious public universities are usually considered [grands établissements](./Grands_établissements). Most of the grandes écoles were relocated to the suburbs of Paris in the 1960s and 1970s, in new campuses much larger than the old campuses within the crowded City of Paris. The [École Normale Supérieure](./École_Normale_Supérieure), [PSL University](./Paris_Sciences_et_Lettres_University) has remained on rue d'Ulm in the [5th arrondissement](./5th_arrondissement_of_Paris).[[332]](./Paris#cite_note-334)
Paris is the home of prestigious universities in science and technology ([Conservatoire national des arts et métiers](./Conservatoire_national_des_arts_et_métiers), [Polytechnic Institute of Paris](./Polytechnic_Institute_of_Paris), [Paris Cité University](./Paris_Cité_University), [Paris-Saclay University](./Paris-Saclay_University), [Sorbonne University](./Sorbonne_University)), political science ([Sciences Po](./Sciences_Po)),[[333]](./Paris#cite_note-335) management ([HEC Paris](./HEC_Paris), [ESSEC Business School](./ESSEC_Business_School), [ESCP Business School](./ESCP_Business_School), [INSEAD](./INSEAD))[[334]](./Paris#cite_note-336) as well as multidisciplinary universities ([Paris Sciences et Lettres University](./Paris_Sciences_et_Lettres_University)).[[335]](./Paris#cite_note-337)

### Healthcare
The [Hôtel-Dieu de Paris](./Hôtel-Dieu_de_Paris) is the oldest hospital in Paris.
Health care and emergency medical service in the City of Paris and its suburbs are provided by the [Assistance publique – Hôpitaux de Paris](./Assistance_publique_–_Hôpitaux_de_Paris) (AP-HP), a public hospital system that employs more than 90,000 people, including practitioners, support personnel, and administrators, in 44 hospitals.[[336]](./Paris#cite_note-hospital-338) It is the largest hospital system in Europe. The hospitals receive more than 5.8 million annual patient visits.[[336]](./Paris#cite_note-hospital-338)
One of the most notable hospitals is the [Hôtel-Dieu](./Hôtel-Dieu_de_Paris), founded in 651, the oldest hospital in Paris and the oldest worldwide still operating,[[337]](./Paris#cite_note-339) although the current building is the product of a reconstruction of 1877. Other hospitals include [Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital](./Pitié-Salpêtrière_Hospital), one of the largest in Europe, [Hôpital Cochin](./Hôpital_Cochin), [Bichat–Claude Bernard Hospital](./Bichat–Claude_Bernard_Hospital), [Hôpital Européen Georges-Pompidou](./Hôpital_Européen_Georges-Pompidou), [Bicêtre Hospital](./Bicêtre_Hospital), [Beaujon Hospital](./Beaujon_Hospital), the [Curie Institute](./Curie_Institute_(Paris)), [Lariboisière Hospital](./Lariboisière_Hospital), [Necker–Enfants Malades Hospital](./Necker–Enfants_Malades_Hospital), [Hôpital Saint-Louis](./Hôpital_Saint-Louis), [Hôpital de la Charité](./Hôpital_de_la_Charité) and the [American Hospital of Paris](./American_Hospital_of_Paris).

##  International relations

### International organisations

The [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](./UNESCO) (UNESCO) has had its headquarters in Paris since November 1958. Paris is also the home of the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](./Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development) (OECD).[[338]](./Paris#cite_note-340) Paris hosts the headquarters of the [European Space Agency](./European_Space_Agency), the [International Energy Agency](./International_Energy_Agency), [European Securities and Markets Authority](./European_Securities_and_Markets_Authority) and the [European Banking Authority](./European_Banking_Authority).

Take notes on one source for a research report. Read all of the source text below; nothing else about it is available to the report.

Question the report must answer: What is the capital of France and roughly its population?

SOURCE: Paris - Wikipedia
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris

This is part 5 of 5 of the source text.

NOTES ALREADY TAKEN from earlier parts of this same source — do not repeat them:
- Paris is a capital city in the Île-de-France region of France. (none stated)
- City population was 2,102,650 in January 2023, down from 2,165,423 in January 2022. (January 2023 and January 2022)
- City population fell by 122,919 (about 5%) between 2013 and 2023. (2013 to 2023)
- Historical peak city population was 2.9 million in 1921; current population is lower. (peak in 1921)
- City population fell from 2,850,000 (1954) to 2,152,000 (1990). (1954 and 1990)
- City population reached 2.25 million in 2011. (2011)
- City population about 2,715,000 by 1901. (1901)
- Paris had 200,000 inhabitants in 1328 and was Europe's most populous city. (1328)
- Population reached 660,000 by 1815 after revolutionary-era drop and post-1799 surge. (1815)
- Population grew from about 400,000 (1640) to 650,000 (1780). (1640 and 1780)
- The Métropole du Grand Paris had 6.945 million people in 2015. (2015, Metropole area of 814 km2)

g/wiki/Conseil_de_Paris) (Council of Paris), which elects the mayor. The council is composed of 163 members. Each arrondissement is allocated many seats, dependent upon its population, from 10 members for each of the least-populated arrondissements to 34 members for the most populated. The council is elected using [closed list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_list) [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation) in a [two-round system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-round_system).[[111]](#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-114)
Party lists winning an absolute [majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority) in the first round – or at least a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting)) in the second round – automatically win half the seats of an arrondissement. The remaining half of the seats are distributed proportionally to all lists which win at least 5% of the vote, using the [highest averages method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_averages_method).[[111]](#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-114) This ensures that the winning party or coalition always wins a majority of the seats, even if they do not win an absolute majority of the vote.[[112]](#cite_note-Pariscouncil-115)
Before the [2020 Paris municipal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Paris_municipal_election), each of Paris's 20 arrondissements had its own town hall and a directly elected council ([conseil d'arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_d'arrondissement)), which elects an arrondissement mayor.[[113]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShales200716-116) The council of each arrondissement is composed of members of the Conseil de Paris, and members who serve only on the council of the arrondissement. The number of deputy mayors in each arrondissement varies depending on its population. As of 1996, there were 20 arrondissement mayors and 120 deputy mayors.[[109]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996334-112) The creation of [Paris Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Centre), a unified administrative division with a single mayor covering the first four arrondissements, took effect with the said 2020 election. The other 16 arrondissements continue to have their own mayors.[[114]](#cite_note-117)

### Métropole du Grand Paris
A map of the Greater Paris Metropolis and its governing territories
In January 2016, the [Métropole du Grand Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Paris) came into existence.[[115]](#cite_note-MGP-118) It is an administrative structure for co-operation between the City of Paris and its nearest suburbs. It includes the City of Paris, plus the communes of the three departments of the inner suburbs, [Hauts-de-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauts-de-Seine), [Seine-Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine-Saint-Denis) and [Val-de-Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val-de-Marne), plus seven communes in the outer suburbs, including [Argenteuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argenteuil) in [Val d'Oise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_d'Oise) and [Paray-Vieille-Poste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paray-Vieille-Poste) in [Essonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essonne), which were added to include the major airports of Paris. The Metropole covers 814 km2 (314 sq mi). In 2015, it had a population of 6.945 million people.[[116]](#cite_note-119)[[117]](#cite_note-lemoniteur1-120)
The new structure is administered by a Metropolitan Council of 210 members, not directly elected, but chosen by the councils of the member Communes. By 2020, its basic competencies will include urban planning, housing, and protection of the environment.[[115]](#cite_note-MGP-118)[[117]](#cite_note-lemoniteur1-120) In January 2016, [Patrick Ollier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Ollier) was elected the first president of the metropolitan council. Though the Metropole has a population of nearly seven million people and accounts for 25 percent of the GDP of France, it has a very small budget: just 65 million Euros, compared with eight billion Euros for the City of Paris.[[118]](#cite_note-121)

### Regional government

The [Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region) of [Île de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_France), including Paris and its surrounding communities, is governed by the [Regional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Council_of_Île-de-France), composed of 209 members representing the different communes. In December 2015, a list of candidates of the Union of the Right, a coalition of centrist and right-wing parties, led by [Valérie Pécresse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valérie_Pécresse), narrowly won the regional election, defeating a coalition of Socialists and ecologists. The Socialists had governed the region for seventeen years. The regional council has 121 members from the Union of the Right, 66 from the Union of the Left and 22 from the extreme right National Front.[[119]](#cite_note-122)

### National government
The [Élysée Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élysée_Palace), official residence of the [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France)
As the capital of France, Paris is the seat of France's [national government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_France). For the executive, the two chief officers each have their own official residences, which also serve as their offices. The [President of the French Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France) resides at the [Élysée Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élysée_Palace).[[120]](#cite_note-123) The [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_France)'s seat is at the [Hôtel Matignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_Matignon).[[121]](#cite_note-124)[[122]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnappWright200693–94-125) Government ministries are located in various parts of the city, many near the Hôtel Matignon.[[123]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorrus2012288-126)
Both houses of the [French Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament) are located on the Rive Gauche. The upper house, the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_(France)), meets in the [Palais du Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_du_Luxembourg). The more important lower house, the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(France)), meets in the [Palais Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Bourbon). The [President of the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Senate_of_France), the second-highest public official in France, with the President of the Republic being the sole superior, resides in the [Petit Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit_Luxembourg), a smaller palace annexe to the Palais du Luxembourg.[[124]](#cite_note-127)The Palais-Royal, residence of the [Conseil d'État](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_d'État_(France))
France's highest courts are located in Paris. The [Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Cassation_(France)), the highest court in the judicial order, which reviews criminal and civil cases, is located in the [Palais de Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_de_Justice,_Paris) on the Île de la Cité.[[125]](#cite_note-128) The [Conseil d'État](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_State_(France)), which provides legal advice to the executive and acts as the highest court in the administrative order, judging litigation against public bodies, is located in the [Palais-Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais-Royal) in the [1st arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_arrondissement_of_Paris).[[126]](#cite_note-129) The [Constitutional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Council_of_France), an advisory body with ultimate authority on the constitutionality of laws and government decrees, meets in the Montpensier wing of the Palais Royal.[[127]](#cite_note-130)
Paris and its region host the headquarters of several international organisations, including [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO), the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development), the [International Chamber of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Chamber_of_Commerce), the [Paris Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Club), the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency), the [International Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Energy_Agency), the [Organisation internationale de la Francophonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_internationale_de_la_Francophonie), the [European Union Institute for Security Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Institute_for_Security_Studies), the [International Bureau of Weights and Measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures), the [International Exhibition Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_International_Expositions), and the [International Federation for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_for_Human_Rights).

## Définitions

Le terme générique de « populations de référence » regroupe pour chaque commune sa
                        population municipale, sa population comptée à part et sa population totale qui est
                        la somme des deux précédentes.
Les populations de référence sont définies par le décret n°2003-485 publié au Journal
                        officiel du 8 juin 2003, relatif au recensement de la population, modifié par le décret
                        n° 2019-1302 du 5 décembre 2019. Désormais, elles sont actualisées et authentifiées
                        par un décret chaque année. Environ 350 textes législatifs ou réglementaires font
                        référence à ces populations.
La population municipale est celle qui est utilisée à des fins statistiques ; la population
                        totale est la plus souvent utilisée pour l'application de dispositions législatives
                        ou réglementaires.
Remarque

                        ce report et continuer à produire des populations de référence de qualité chaque année.

La population comptée à part comprend certaines personnes dont la résidence habituelle est dans une autre

Les définitions des nouvelles populations de référence ont évolué par rapport à celles en vigueur lors du
recensement de la population de 1999.
Les principaux changements affectant les définitions des populations sont les suivants :
Il  n’y  a  plus  de  différence  entre  les  notions  de  population  municipale  et  de  population  sans  doubles
comptes.
La nouvelle définition de la population municipale est proche de l’ancienne à l’exception :
La population comptée à part est affectée de façon symétrique par les changements évoqués plus haut
concernant la population municipale.
Les  personnes  majeures  âgées  de  25  ans  ou  plus  ayant  leur  résidence  familiale  sur  le  territoire  de  la
commune  et  qui  résident  dans  une  autre  commune  pour  leurs  études  ne  sont  plus  comptées  dans  la
population comptée à part de la commune de leur résidence familiale. Elles ne sont donc plus comptées
dans  la  population  totale.  C’est  le  seul  changement  notable  affectant  cette  dernière,  les  autres
correspondant  à  des  transferts  entre  population  municipale  et  population  comptée  à  part.
des  étudiants  majeurs  vivant  dans  un  établissement  d’enseignement  situé  dans  la  commune  mais
ayant  leur  résidence  familiale  dans  une  autre  commune  :  ils  sont  désormais  comptés  dans  la
population  municipale  de  la  commune  d’études  et,  s’ils  ont  moins  de  25  ans,  dans  la  population
comptée  à  part  de  la  commune  de  résidence  familiale  ;
des  militaires  logés  dans  un  établissement  d’enseignement  militaire,  dans  une  caserne,  un  quartier,
une  base  ou  un  camp  militaire  :  ils  sont  désormais  comptés  dans  la  population  municipale  de  la
commune sur laquelle est située cette structure et dans la population comptée à part de la commune
de leur résidence familiale lorsqu’ils en ont une ;
des  personnes  détenues  dans  un  établissement  pénitentiaire  de  la  commune  qui  sont  désormais
comptées  dans  la  population  municipale  ;
des  étudiants  mineurs  logés  dans  la  commune,  dans  une  cité  universitaire,  un  foyer  d’étudiants  ou
hors communauté, et ayant leur résidence familiale dans une autre commune : désormais ils ne sont
plus comptés dans la population municipale de la commune mais dans la population comptée à part.

The city of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris) (also called the Commune or Department of Paris) had a population of 2,047,602 people within its administrative city limits as of 1 January 2026.[[1]](#cite_note-paris_pop_2023-1) It is surrounded by the Paris [unité urbaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unité_urbaine), or urban area, the [most populous urban area in the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_urban_areas_of_the_European_Union).
In 2023 the unité urbaine had a population of 11,013,774 in 2,824 km2 (1,090 sq mi).[[2]](#cite_note-pop-2) The Paris Region, or [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France), covers 12,012 km2 (4,638 sq mi), and has its own regional council and president. It has a population of 12,463,067 as of January 2023, or 18.3 percent of the population of France.[[2]](#cite_note-pop-2) The metropolitan or [functional area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_area_(France)) (aire d'attraction) of Paris covers 18,941 km2 (7,313 sq mi) and has 13,320,752 inhabitants (2023).[[2]](#cite_note-pop-2)
The population of the city of Paris reached a historic high of 2.9 million in 1921 but then declined; between 1954 and 1999 it declined at every census, falling to 2,125,246 in 1999.[[3]](#cite_note-3) After that it began to climb again, reaching 2,240,621 in 2012, but falling to 2,103,778 in 2023.[[1]](#cite_note-paris_pop_2023-1)
The city's population loss reflected the experience of most other core cities in the developed world that have not expanded their boundaries. The principal factors in the process were a significant decline in household size, and a dramatic migration of residents to the suburbs between 1962 and 1975.  Factors in the migration included [deindustrialisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deindustrialization), high rent, the [gentrification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentrification) of many inner quarters, the transformation of living space into offices, and greater affluence among working families. The city's population loss was one of the most severe among international municipalities and the largest for any that had achieved more than 2,000,000 residents. Since then, an influx of younger residents and immigrants has contributed to the growth of the city.

## Density
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=1)]Paris population pyramid in 2022
According to [Eurostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostat), the EU statistical agency, in 2012 the Commune of Paris was the most densely populated city in the European Union, with 21,616 people per square kilometre within the city limits (the NUTS-3 statistical area),  ahead of Inner London West, which had 10,374 persons per square kilometre.  According to the same census, three departments bordering Paris, [Hauts-de-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauts-de-Seine), [Seine-Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine-Saint-Denis) and [Val-de-Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val-de-Marne), had population densities of over ten thousand persons per square kilometre, ranking among the ten most densely populated areas of the EU.[[4]](#cite_note-4)
Paris is one of the most densely populated cities in the world.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMadgeWillmott200611-5) Its density, excluding the outlying woodland parks of [Boulogne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Boulogne) and [Vincennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bois_de_Vincennes), was 24,448 inhabitants per square kilometre (63,320/sq mi) in the 1999 official census, which could be compared only with some [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia) [megapolises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalopolis_(city_type)) and the [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) [borough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borough_(New_York_City)) of [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan). Even including the two woodland areas, its population density was 20,755/km2 (53,760/sq mi) in 2017,[[6]](#cite_note-compparis-6) the sixth-most-densely populated commune in France after [Levallois-Perret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levallois-Perret), [Vincennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincennes), [Le Pré-Saint-Gervais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Pré-Saint-Gervais), [Saint-Mandé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Mandé) and [Montrouge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montrouge), all of which border the city proper.[[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)]
The most sparsely populated quarters are the western and central office and administration-focused [arrondissements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissements_of_Paris). The city's population is densest in the northern and eastern arrondissements; the [11th arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_arrondissement_of_Paris) had a density of 40,672 inhabitants per square kilometre (105,340/sq mi) in 1999, and some of the same arrondissement's eastern quarters had densities close to 100,000/km2 (260,000/sq mi) in the same year.Population density map of Paris in January 2017

## Paris agglomeration
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=2)]Population density map of the Île-de-France region (2023 population data)
The city of Paris covers an area much smaller than the urban area of which it is the core. At present, Paris's real urbanisation, defined by the [pôle urbain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pôle_urbain) (urban cluster) statistical area, covers 2,845 km2 (1,098 sq mi),[[8]](#cite_note-UU_superficie-8) or an area about 27 times larger than the city itself. The administration of Paris's urban growth is divided between itself and its surrounding departments: Paris's closest ring of three adjoining departments, or petite couronne ("small ring") are fully saturated with urban growth, and the ring of four departments outside of these, the grande couronne departments, are only covered in their inner regions by Paris's urbanisation. These eight departments form the larger administrative Île-de-France région; most of this region is filled, and overextended in places, by the Paris [functional area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_area), which, in 2023, was populated by over 13 million people.[[9]](#cite_note-pop_AAV-9)
The Paris agglomeration has shown a steady rate of growth since the end of the late 16th century [French Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion), save brief setbacks during the French Revolution and World War II. With 13.3 million inhabitants in 2023, the annual population growth rate of the Paris functional area was between 0.4% and 1.0% over the past 55 years.[[9]](#cite_note-pop_AAV-9)

By law, French censuses do not ask questions regarding ethnicity or religion, but do gather information concerning one's country of birth. From this it is still possible to determine that Paris and its metropolitan area is one of the most multi-cultural in Europe: According to the 2011 census, 456,105 residents of the municipality of Paris, or 20.3 percent,  and 2,117,901 residents of the Paris Region (Île-de-France), or 17.9 percent, were born outside France.[[12]](#cite_note-12)  At the 1999 census, 4.2% of the population in Paris [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Area_(France)) were recent immigrants (people who had immigrated to France between 1990 and 1999), the majority from [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia) and [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa). 37 % of all immigrants in France live in the Paris region.[[13]](#cite_note-riot-13)
The first wave of international migration to Paris started as early as 1820, with the arrivals of German peasants fleeing an agricultural crisis in their homeland. Several waves of immigration followed continually until today: Italians and central European Jews during the 19th century; Russians after the [revolution of 1917](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Revolution_of_1917) and Armenians fleeing [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide) in the Ottoman Empire;[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHassell199122-14) colonial subjects during [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I) and later;[[15]](#cite_note-15) Poles between the two world wars; Spaniards, Italians, Portuguese, and North Africans from the 1950s to the 1970s; North African Jews after colonies in that region gained independence; Africans and Asians since then.[[16]](#cite_note-past_immigration-16)
The Paris metropolitan region, or aire urbaine, is estimated to be home to some 1.7 million Muslims, who comprise between 10–15 per cent of the area's population. However, without official data, the margin of error of these estimates is extremely high as it is based on one's country of birth (someone born in a Muslim country or born to a parent from a Muslim country is considered as a "potential Muslim").[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZarkaTaussigFleury200427-17) According to the North American Jewish Data Bank, an estimated 310,000 Jews also live in Paris and the surrounding Île-de-France region, an area with a population of 11.7 million. Paris has historically been a magnet for immigrants, and it hosts one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in Europe today.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

### Africans

As of 2012 tens of thousands of people of African origins live in Paris. This group includes those born in France who had African parents and naturalized French citizens born in Africa. The majority come from the [Maghreb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maghreb), including [Algeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria), [Morocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco), and [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia). Other countries with populations in Paris include [Burkina Faso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burkina_Faso), the [Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo), [Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinea), [Mali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mali), and [Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegal).[[23]](#cite_note-23)

### Asians
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=8)]
As of 1998 [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France) has half of the Asian population of France.[[24]](#cite_note-Guillonp186-24) As of 1990 the majority of Asians living in France are [ethnic Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese) originating from several countries.[[25]](#cite_note-Guillonp187-25)
In 1974 France stopped allowing foreign workers into its borders. The Asian population of France increased despite the closure. In 1975 there were 20,000 Asians in Île-de-France. In 1982 the region had 59,000. This increased to 108,000 in 1990.[[25]](#cite_note-Guillonp187-25)
In France the "Asians" are defined as people originating from the [East Asian cultural sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asian_cultural_sphere). The term does not include people from the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent).[[24]](#cite_note-Guillonp186-24)

#### Geography of the Asian population
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=9)]
For the entire [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France) region, there were a total of 108,511 persons who held or formerly held Cambodian, Chinese, Laotian, Taiwanese, and Vietnamese citizenships as of 1990. This included 64,361 current citizens of those countries and 44,150 former citizens who became naturalized as French citizens.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)
As of 1990, there were a combined total of 31,773 persons who held or formerly held Cambodian, Chinese, Laotian, Taiwanese, and Vietnamese citizenships in the City of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris). This included 21,655 current citizens of those countries and 10,118 former citizens who became naturalized as French citizens.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)
As of 1990 fewer than 10,000 persons of East/Southeast Asian origin resided in six communes of [Marne-la-Vallée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marne-la-Vallée). 26% of the population of [Lognes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lognes) was Asian, and other percentages were 8% in [Noisiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noisiel), 5–6% in [Noisy-le-Grand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noisy-le-Grand), and 5–6% in [Torcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torcy,_Seine-et-Marne). In 1982 there were 6,000 Asians in Marne-la-Vallée, making up 3–4% of the area's population. In 1987 the number increased to 9,000.[[27]](#cite_note-Guillonp198-27)
As of circa 1998 [Ivry-sur-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivry-sur-Seine) and [Vitry-sur-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitry-sur-Seine) had a combined Asian population of 3,600.[[28]](#cite_note-Guillonp197-28)
As of circa 1998 there were about 6,000 East/Southeast Asians in and around [Aulnay-sous-Bois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aulnay-sous-Bois), and there were 3,000 persons of East and Southeast Asian origin in Aulnay proper. Most of them were of [Cambodian origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_French), including those with and without Cambodian citizenship. The commune also had an above-average number of [persons of Laotian origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laotians_in_France), including those with and without Laotian citizenship. Ethnicities included [Khmer people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmer_people), [Lao people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lao_people), and [Overseas Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overseas_Chinese).[[28]](#cite_note-Guillonp197-28)

#### Cambodians
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=10)]
As of 1990, in the City of Paris there were 7,950 Cambodian citizens and 3,279 former Cambodian citizens who became naturalized as French. The combined total is 11,229.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)

#### Chinese
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=11)]
Main article: [Chinese community in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_community_in_Paris)The Olympiades towers with the pagoda roof shopping centre, [Chinatown, Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown,_Paris)
As of 1990 the majority of Asians living in the Paris area are [ethnic Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overseas_Chinese) originating from several countries.[[25]](#cite_note-Guillonp187-25) The largest group includes ethnic Chinese from [Indochina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochina), and a smaller group originates from [Zhejiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhejiang).[[29]](#cite_note-Guillonp189-29)

#### Japanese
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=12)]
Main article: [Japanese community in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_community_in_Paris)
As of 2013 the official number of Japanese residents in Paris was 16,277.[[30]](#cite_note-ConteHelmp81-30)

#### Laotians
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=13)]
As of 1990, in the City of Paris there were 2,185 Laotian citizens and 1,376 former Laotian citizens naturalized as French, making a combined total of 3,561.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)
As of that year, in the Île-de-France region there were 10,110 Laotian citizens and 8,177 former Laotian citizens, making a combined total of 18,287.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)

#### Vietnamese
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=14)]
Main article: [Vietnamese community in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_community_in_Paris)
In periods before 1975 several Vietnamese arrived in Paris, including intellectuals, those who worked as civil servants in colonial times, and those who came to Paris to study and did not return home. Ethnic Vietnamese arriving after 1975 became a part of an ethnic network established by those that came before them. Many Vietnamese achieved proficiency in the medical, scientific, and computer science fields.[[31]](#cite_note-Guillonp190-31)
As of 1990, in the City of Paris there were 3,802 Vietnamese citizens and 4,155 former Vietnamese citizens naturalized as French, making a total of 7,957.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)
As of that year, in the Île-de-France region there were 16,387 Vietnamese citizens and 20,261 former Vietnamese citizens naturalized as French, making a total of 36,648.[[26]](#cite_note-Guillonp188-26)

#### Romani
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Demographics_of_Paris&action=edit&section=15)]
See also: [Deportation of Roma migrants from France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportation_of_Roma_migrants_from_France)
[Romani people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romani_people) first arrived in Paris in 1427.[[32]](#cite_note-32)
