## Définitions

Toutes les définitions des concepts utilisés sont accessibles dans la [rubrique définitions](/fr/metadonnees/definitions)
Concernant spécifiquement le recensement de la population, se référer à [la définition des concepts du recensement de la population](/fr/information/2383278)

## Champ

### Recensements de la population

Les données sont proposées aux utilisateurs notamment pour
                     comparer des communes, regrouper des modalités de variables ou obtenir
                     des résultats sur des ensembles personnalisés de communes.
Issues de calculs liés aux techniques d’échantillonnage, les
                     données en effectifs sont fournies avec plusieurs décimales ; celles-ci
                     doivent être utilisées pour tous les calculs réalisés, de façon à éviter
                     les erreurs d’arrondis.
Pour avoir plus d’information sur le recensement de la
                     population, consultez la page de [présentation du recensement de la
                        population](/fr/information/2383265).
Les données proviennent soit de l’exploitation principale
                     (princ), soit de l’exploitation complémentaire (compl).
Pour plus d’information méthodologique, vous pouvez consulter
                     les fiches ["Conseils pour
                        l’utilisation des résultats du recensement"](/fr/information/2383177).
Ces fiches présentent les caractéristiques du recensement de la
                     population et traitent de leurs conséquences sur l’utilisation des
                     données. Elles précisent en particulier les changements affectant les
                     principales variables statistiques et leur comparabilité avec les
                     recensements précédents.

### État civil

Les statistiques annuelles concernant les naissances
                     domiciliées sont dressées à partir des bulletins
                     statistiques de l’état civil, établis par les maires, au moment et dans
                     la commune où ont lieu les naissances. Elles portent sur les naissances
                     ayant eu lieu dans toutes les communes de France. Les naissances ayant
                     eu lieu à l’étranger ou dans les COM ne sont pas comptabilisées.
La variable "commune" correspond à la commune du domicile de la
                     mère en France.
Les statistiques comprennent les jugements déclaratifs de
                     naissance, mais ne prennent pas en compte les enfants mort-nés.

Les statistiques annuelles concernant les décès
                     domiciliés sont dressées à partir des bulletins
                     statistiques de l’état civil, établis par les maires, au moment et dans
                     la commune où ont lieu les décès. Elles portent sur les décès ayant eu
                     lieu dans toutes les communes de France. Les décès ayant eu lieu à
                     l’étranger ou dans les COM ne sont pas comptabilisés.
La variable "commune" correspond à la commune du domicile du
                     défunt en France.
Les statistiques comprennent les jugements déclaratifs de décès.

### Fichier Localisé Social et Fiscal (Filosofi)

Le champ porte sur les personnes appartenant à des ménages
                     fiscaux ordinaires dont le revenu disponible est positif ou nul.
Les résultats couvrent la France métropolitaine et La Réunion.

### Base Tous Salariés (BTS)

Le champ correspond aux salariés du privé, y compris alternants,
                     stagiaires et bénéficiaires de contrats aidés, hors salariés de l’agriculture
                     et des particuliers employeurs.

### Système d’information sur la démographie d’entreprises (Side)

Les indicateurs portent sur les créations et les stocks
                     d’entreprises et d’établissements de l’ensemble des activités
                     productives et marchandes non agricoles. Ce champ inclut les activités
                     financières.
Quand on parle d’entreprises, tous les dénombrements portent en
                     réalité sur des unités légales pour cette source. Lorsqu’une unité
                     légale comprend plusieurs établissements, elle est localisée à son
                     siège.
Le nombre de créations d’entreprises ou d’établissements
                     correspond au nombre d’unités légales ou d’établissements créés au cours
                     de l’année N.
Le nombre d’entreprises ou d’établissements de l’année N
                     correspond au nombre d’unités légales ou d’établissements économiquement
                     actifs en N.

### Fichier localisé des rémunérations et de l’emploi salarié (Flores)

Le dispositif Flores (Fichier localisé des rémunérations et de
                     l’emploi salarié) couvre les établissements ayant employé au moins un
                     salarié pendant l’année, en France. Dans cette base
                     communale, les données mises à disposition sont par ailleurs restreintes
                     aux établissements actifs en fin d’année (dernière semaine de décembre),
                     ce qui exclut les établissements qui ont cessé leur activité en cours
                     d’année.
L’effectif salarié en fin d’année correspond au nombre de postes
                     présents la dernière semaine de décembre dans l’établissement employeur.
                     L’effectif en fin d’année de certains établissements peut donc être nul,
                     si le ou les personnes salariées pendant l’année n’étaient plus en
                     emploi fin décembre.
Flores couvre l’ensemble de l’emploi salarié, quel que soit le
                     secteur d’activité et le type d’employeur (public ou privé, y compris
                     les particuliers employeurs). Sont exclus du champ les établissements
                     relevant du ministère des Armées (personnels militaires comme civils).

### Base permanente des équipements (BPE)

La base permanente des équipements (BPE) est une base à vocation
                     statistique. Elle répertorie un large éventail d’équipements et de
                     services, marchands ou non, accessibles au public sur l’ensemble de la
                     France au 1ᵉʳ janvier de chaque année.
La base permanente des équipements (BPE) est un dispositif
                     alimenté par différentes sources : [sources
                        utilisées par la BPE](/fr/metadonnees/source/operation/s2216/processus-statistique).

### Tourisme

Le champ porte sur les hôtels de tourisme, classés ou pas, de
                     plus de 5
                     chambres et sur les campings de plus de 10 emplacements, classés ou pas,
                     y compris les
                     campings résidentiels. Il porte également sur les autres hébergements
                     collectifs
                     touristiques.
Les statistiques sur l’offre d’hébergements sont établies en
                     relation avec
                     les comités régionaux de tourisme (CRT). Elles sont proposées au niveau
                     communal pour
                     la France (hors Mayotte).
Les statistiques concernant l’hôtellerie de plein air portent
                     sur les
                     campings offrant des emplacements à la clientèle de passage destinés aux
                     touristes n’y
                     élisant pas domicile ainsi que sur les campings proposant des
                     emplacements loués à
                     l’année, c’est à-dire à un seul client pour l’ensemble de la période
                     d’ouverture du
                     camping.
Les hôtels et les campings classés le sont selon la nouvelle
                     nomenclature de
                     classification mise en œuvre par l’opérateur Atout France.

### Répertoire électoral unique

Le Répertoire électoral unique couvre l’ensemble des territoires
                     français à l’exception de la Nouvelle-Calédonie.
Le champ porte sur les électeurs inscrits sur la liste
                     électo

## Champ

### Recensements de la population

Les données sont proposées aux utilisateurs notamment pour
                     comparer des communes, regrouper des modalités de variables ou obtenir
                     des résultats sur des ensembles personnalisés de communes.
Issues de calculs liés aux techniques d’échantillonnage, les
                     données en effectifs sont fournies avec plusieurs décimales ; celles-ci
                     doivent être utilisées pour tous les calculs réalisés, de façon à éviter
                     les erreurs d’arrondis.
Pour avoir plus d’information sur le recensement de la
                     population, consultez la page de [présentation du recensement de la
                        population](/fr/information/2383265).
Les données proviennent soit de l’exploitation principale
                     (princ), soit de l’exploitation complémentaire (compl).
Pour plus d’information méthodologique, vous pouvez consulter
                     les fiches ["Conseils pour
                        l’utilisation des résultats du recensement"](/fr/information/2383177).
Ces fiches présentent les caractéristiques du recensement de la
                     population et traitent de leurs conséquences sur l’utilisation des
                     données. Elles précisent en particulier les changements affectant les
                     principales variables statistiques et leur comparabilité avec les
                     recensements précédents.

### État civil

Les statistiques annuelles concernant les naissances
                     domiciliées sont dressées à partir des bulletins
                     statistiques de l’état civil, établis par les maires, au moment et dans
                     la commune où ont lieu les naissances. Elles portent sur les naissances
                     ayant eu lieu dans toutes les communes de France. Les naissances ayant
                     eu lieu à l’étranger ou dans les COM ne sont pas comptabilisées.
La variable "commune" correspond à la commune du domicile de la
                     mère en France.
Les statistiques comprennent les jugements déclaratifs de
                     naissance, mais ne prennent pas en compte les enfants mort-nés.

Les statistiques annuelles concernant les décès
                     domiciliés sont dressées à partir des bulletins
                     statistiques de l’état civil, établis par les maires, au moment et dans
                     la commune où ont lieu les décès. Elles portent sur les décès ayant eu
                     lieu dans toutes les communes de France. Les décès ayant eu lieu à
                     l’étranger ou dans les COM ne sont pas comptabilisés.
La variable "commune" correspond à la commune du domicile du
                     défunt en France.
Les statistiques comprennent les jugements déclaratifs de décès.

### Fichier Localisé Social et Fiscal (Filosofi)

Le champ porte sur les personnes appartenant à des ménages
                     fiscaux ordinaires dont le revenu disponible est positif ou nul.
Les résultats couvrent la France métropolitaine et La Réunion.

### Base Tous Salariés (BTS)

Le champ correspond aux salariés du privé, y compris alternants,
                     stagiaires et bénéficiaires de contrats aidés, hors salariés de l’agriculture
                     et des particuliers employeurs.

### Système d’information sur la démographie d’entreprises (Side)

Les indicateurs portent sur les créations et les stocks
                     d’entreprises et d’établissements de l’ensemble des activités
                     productives et marchandes non agricoles. Ce champ inclut les activités
                     financières.
Quand on parle d’entreprises, tous les dénombrements portent en
                     réalité sur des unités légales pour cette source. Lorsqu’une unité
                     légale comprend plusieurs établissements, elle est localisée à son
                     siège.
Le nombre de créations d’entreprises ou d’établissements
                     correspond au nombre d’unités légales ou d’établissements créés au cours
                     de l’année N.
Le nombre d’entreprises ou d’établissements de l’année N
                     correspond au nombre d’unités légales ou d’établissements économiquement
                     actifs en N.

### Fichier localisé des rémunérations et de l’emploi salarié (Flores)

Le dispositif Flores (Fichier localisé des rémunérations et de
                     l’emploi salarié) couvre les établissements ayant employé au moins un
                     salarié pendant l’année, en France. Dans cette base
                     communale, les données mises à disposition sont par ailleurs restreintes
                     aux établissements actifs en fin d’année (dernière semaine de décembre),
                     ce qui exclut les établissements qui ont cessé leur activité en cours
                     d’année.
L’effectif salarié en fin d’année correspond au nombre de postes
                     présents la dernière semaine de décembre dans l’établissement employeur.
                     L’effectif en fin d’année de certains établissements peut donc être nul,
                     si le ou les personnes salariées pendant l’année n’étaient plus en
                     emploi fin décembre.
Flores couvre l’ensemble de l’emploi salarié, quel que soit le
                     secteur d’activité et le type d’employeur (public ou privé, y compris
                     les particuliers employeurs). Sont exclus du champ les établissements
                     relevant du ministère des Armées (personnels militaires comme civils).

### Base permanente des équipements (BPE)

La base permanente des équipements (BPE) est une base à vocation
                     statistique. Elle répertorie un large éventail d’équipements et de
                     services, marchands ou non, accessibles au public sur l’ensemble de la
                     France au 1ᵉʳ janvier de chaque année.
La base permanente des équipements (BPE) est un dispositif
                     alimenté par différentes sources : [sources
                        utilisées par la BPE](/fr/metadonnees/source/operation/s2216/processus-statistique).

### Tourisme

Le champ porte sur les hôtels de tourisme, classés ou pas, de
                     plus de 5
                     chambres et sur les campings de plus de 10 emplacements, classés ou pas,
                     y compris les
                     campings résidentiels. Il porte également sur les autres hébergements
                     collectifs
                     touristiques.
Les statistiques sur l’offre d’hébergements sont établies en
                     relation avec
                     les comités régionaux de tourisme (CRT). Elles sont proposées au niveau
                     communal pour
                     la France (hors Mayotte).
Les statistiques concernant l’hôtellerie de plein air portent
                     sur les
                     campings offrant des emplacements à la clientèle de passage destinés aux
                     touristes n’y
                     élisant pas domicile ainsi que sur les campings proposant des
                     emplacements loués à
                     l’année, c’est à-dire à un seul client pour l’ensemble de la période
                     d’ouverture du
                     camping.
Les hôtels et les campings classés le sont selon la nouvelle
                     nomenclature de
                     classification mise en œuvre par l’opérateur Atout France.

The Paris metropolitan area ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language): Aire urbaine de Paris) is a [statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_area_(France)) that describes the reach of commuter movement to and from [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France) and its surrounding suburbs.

## Overview
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Paris_metropolitan_area&action=edit&section=1)]
In 2020, France's national [INSEE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_national_de_la_statistique_et_des_études_économiques) statistical bureau introduced the concept "aire d'attraction d'une ville" ([functional area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_area_(France))), replacing the former "aire urbaine" ([urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area_(France))).[[2]](#cite_note-defaav-2) A functional area consists of an urban cluster[[3]](#cite_note-3) and the surrounding commuting zone.[[2]](#cite_note-defaav-2) This concept is consistent with the [functional urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larger_urban_zone) as defined by [Eurostat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurostat).[[4]](#cite_note-4)
Created and used from 1996 by France's national INSEE statistical bureau to match international demographic standards,[[5]](#cite_note-Hatier-5) the aire urbaine (literally: 'urban area') was a statistical unit that described the suburban development around centres of urban growth.[[6]](#cite_note-6) In 2011, the INSEE reclassified its largest aires urbaines into aires métropolitaines (literally: metropolitan areas) and grandes aires urbaines ('large urban areas').[[7]](#cite_note-INSEE-7) With this change, the Paris metropolitan area became the largest in France.[[8]](#cite_note-rang_AU-8)
In France, use of the term 'Paris metropolitan area' is limited to demographic and statistical studies, and, to date, it is not used in economic statistics — the traditional administrative subdivisions commune, département, and région are still referenced for this — though the media will employ it when referring to the electoral tendencies of France's largest cities[[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)]. In 2010 the government passed a law that invited France's largest city 'metropoles' to work together as an intercommunitary entities (more or less described by the INSEE concept),[[9]](#cite_note-9) but the lack of response by the following year moved the government to make the cooperation for many of France's largest cities obligatory, and Paris became a case study all on its own.[[10]](#cite_note-10)
This latter initiative created the "[Métropole du Grand Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Paris)" (official translation: 'Greater Paris metropolitan authority'), a Paris-centred intercommunal cooperation effort enacted from January 1, 2016.[[11]](#cite_note-metropolegrandparis.fr-11) The territory it covers is much smaller than the INSEE 'Paris metropolitan area' statistical area: it includes Paris, its neighbouring three departments (or '[petite couronne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France#Petite_Couronne)'), and a few bordering communes in the departments beyond.[[12]](#cite_note-Carte_des_territoires-12)

## Extent
[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Paris_metropolitan_area&action=edit&section=2)]Map showing the extent of the Paris metropolitan area at the 1999 census, when it included 1,584 [communes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France) and covered 14,518 km2.[False-color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_color) satellite image of the Parisian metropolitan area.
As of 2022, the INSEE statistical [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris) metropolitan area covers 1,929 communes.[[13]](#cite_note-cog-13) With its 18,941 km2 (7,313 sq mi), it extends significantly beyond Paris' administrative [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France) [region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_France) (12,012 km2 (4,638 sq mi)).[[14]](#cite_note-compar-14) Outside the Île-de-France region, it covers part of the departments [Aisne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aisne), [Aube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aube), [Eure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eure), [Eure-et-Loir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eure-et-Loir), [Loiret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loiret), [Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marne_(department)), [Oise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oise), [Seine-Maritime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine-Maritime) and [Yonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonne).[[13]](#cite_note-cog-13)
The Paris metropolitan area expands at each population census due to the rapid population growth in the Paris area. New [communes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France) (municipalities) surrounding Paris are included when they meet the commuter threshold required. At the 1968 census, the earliest date for which population figures were retrospectively computed for French aire urbaines, the Paris metropolitan area had 8,368,459 inhabitants in an area that only encompassed 279 communes in central Île-de-France.[[15]](#cite_note-Julien-15)
By the 1999 census the Paris metropolitan area was slightly larger than Île-de-France and had 11,174,743 inhabitants in 14,518 km2. At the 2010 revision, the aire urbaine of Paris had 1,750 communes.[[16]](#cite_note-meta-16)

##  Etymology

The ancient [oppidum](./Oppidum) that corresponds to the modern city of Paris was first mentioned in the mid-1st century BC by [Julius Caesar](./Julius_Caesar) as Lutetia Parisiorum ('[Lutetia](./Lutetia) of the [Parisii](./Parisii_(France))') and is later attested as Parision in the 5th century AD, then as Paris in 1265.[[7]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTENègre1990155-8)[[8]](./Paris#cite_note-Falileyev-9) During the Roman period, it was commonly known as Lutetia in Latin, which is interpreted as either stemming from the [Celtic](./Celtic_languages) root *lukot- ('mouse'), or from *luto- ('marsh, swamp').[[9]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELambert199438-10)[[10]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelamarre2003211-11)[[8]](./Paris#cite_note-Falileyev-9)
The name Paris is derived from its early inhabitants, the [Parisii](./Parisii_(France)), a [Gallic](./Gauls) tribe from the [Iron Age](./La_Tène_culture) and the [Roman period](./Roman_period).[[11]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelamarre2003247-12) The meaning of the Gaulish [ethnonym](./Ethnonym) remains debated. According to [Xavier Delamarre](./Xavier_Delamarre), it may derive from the Celtic root pario- ('cauldron').[[11]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDelamarre2003247-12) [Alfred Holder](./Alfred_Holder) interpreted the name as 'the makers' or 'the commanders', by comparing it to the [Welsh](./Welsh_language) peryff ('lord, commander'), both possibly descending from a [Proto-Celtic](./Proto-Celtic) form reconstructed as *kwar-is-io-.[[12]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBusse2006199-13) Alternatively, [Pierre-Yves Lambert](./Pierre-Yves_Lambert) proposed to translate Parisii as the 'spear people', by connecting the first element to the [Old Irish](./Old_Irish) carr ('spear'), derived from an earlier *kwar-sā.[[8]](./Paris#cite_note-Falileyev-9)
Residents of the city are known in English as Parisians and in French as Parisiens ([[paʁizjɛ̃]](./Help:IPA/French) [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Parisien2.ogg)). They are also pejoratively called Parigots ([[paʁiɡo]](./Help:IPA/French) [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Parigot.ogg)).[[13]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDottin2018535-14)

##  History

Main article: [History of Paris](./History_of_Paris)
For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Paris](./Timeline_of_Paris).

### Origins

Main article: [Lutetia](./Lutetia)
The [Parisii](./Parisii_(Gaul)) people inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BC.[[14]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTECunliffe2004201-15) One of the area's major north–south trade routes crossed the [Seine](./Seine) on the [Île de la Cité](./Île_de_la_Cité), which gradually became an important trading centre.[[15]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201025-16) The Parisii traded with many river towns (some as far away as the Iberian Peninsula) and minted their own coins.[[16]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt200965–70-17)Gold coins minted by the [Parisii](./Parisii_(Gaul)), 1st century BC
[Julius Caesar](./Julius_Caesar) [conquered](./Gallic_Wars) the [Paris Basin](./Paris_Basin) for the [Roman Republic](./Roman_Republic) in 52 BC and began the Roman settlement on Paris's [Left Bank](./Rive_Gauche).[[17]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt200988–104-18) The Roman town was originally called [Lutetia](./Lutetia) (more fully, Lutetia Parisiorum, "Lutetia of the Parisii", modern French Lutèce). It became a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres, and an [amphitheatre](./Amphitheatre).[[18]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009154–167-19)
By the end of the [Western Roman Empire](./Western_Roman_Empire), the town was known as Parisius, a [Latin](./Latin_language) name that would later become Paris in French.[[19]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeunier201412-20) [Christianity](./Christianity) was introduced in the middle of the 3rd century AD by Saint [Denis](./Saint_Denis_of_Paris), the first Bishop of Paris: according to legend, when he refused to renounce his faith before the Roman occupiers, he was beheaded on the hill which became known as Mons Martyrum (Latin "Hill of Martyrs"), later "[Montmartre](./Montmartre)", from where he walked headless to the north of the city; the place where he fell and was buried became an important religious shrine, the [Basilica of Saint-Denis](./Basilica_of_Saint-Denis), and many French kings are buried there.[[20]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009210–211-21)The [Wall of Philippe Auguste](./Wall_of_Philip_II_Augustus), oldest city wall in Paris
[Clovis the Frank](./Clovis_I), the first king of the [Merovingian dynasty](./Merovingian_dynasty), made the city his capital from 508.[[21]](./Paris#cite_note-22) As the Frankish domination of Gaul began, there was a gradual immigration by the [Franks](./Franks) to Paris, and the Parisian [Francien](./Francien_language) dialects were born. Fortification of the [Île de la Cité](./Île_de_la_Cité) failed to avert [sacking by Vikings in 845](./Siege_of_Paris_(845)). Still, Paris's strategic importance—with its bridges preventing ships from passing—was established by successful defence in the [Siege of Paris (885–886)](./Siege_of_Paris_(885–886)), for which the then [Count of Paris](./Count_of_Paris) (comte de Paris), [Odo of France](./Odo_of_France), was elected king of [West Francia](./West_Francia).[[22]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones199448-23) From the [Capetian](./House_of_Capet) dynasty that began with the 987 election of [Hugh Capet](./Hugh_Capet), Count of Paris and [Duke of the Franks](./Duke_of_the_Franks) (duc des Francs), as king of a unified West Francia, Paris gradually became the largest and most prosperous city in France.[[20]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009210–211-21)

### High and Late Middle Ages to Louis XIV

See also: [Paris in the Middle Ages](./Paris_in_the_Middle_Ages), [Paris in the 16th century](./Paris_in_the_16th_century), and [Paris in the 17th century](./Paris_in_the_17th_century)The [Palais de la Cité](./Palais_de_la_Cité) and [Sainte-Chapelle](./Sainte-Chapelle), viewed from the Left Bank, from the [Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry](./Très_Riches_Heures_du_duc_de_Berry) (month of June) (1410)
By the end of the 12th century, Paris had become the political, economic, religious, and cultural capital of France.[[23]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201027-24) [Maurice de Sully](./Maurice_de_Sully), bishop of Paris, started the construction of the [Notre Dame Cathedral](./Notre_Dame_de_Paris) in 1163, and was completed after 182 years.[[24]](./Paris#cite_note-25) After the marshland between the river Seine and its slower 'dead arm' to its north was filled in[[clarification needed](./Wikipedia:Please_clarify)] from around the 10th century,[[25]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBussmann198522-26) Paris's cultural centre began to move to the Right Bank. In 1137, a new city marketplace (today's [Les Halles](./Les_Halles)) replaced the two smaller ones on the Île de la Cité and [Place de Grève (Place de l'Hôtel de Ville)](./Place_de_l'Hôtel-de-Ville_–_Esplanade_de_la_Libération).[[26]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_VitriacoHinnebusch1972262-27) The latter location housed the headquarters of Paris's river trade corporation. This organisation later became, unofficially (although formally in later years), Paris's first municipal government.
In the late 12th century, [Philip Augustus](./Philip_II_of_France) extended the [Louvre](./Louvre) fortress to defend the city against river invasions from the west, gave the city its first walls between 1190 and 1215, rebuilt its bridges to either side of its central island, and paved its main thoroughfares.[[27]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarmant201236–40-28) In 1190, he transformed Paris's former cathedral school into a student-teacher corporation that would become the [University of Paris](./University_of_Paris) and would draw students from all of Europe.[[28]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarmant201228–29-29)[[23]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201027-24)
With 200,000 inhabitants in 1328, Paris, then already the capital of France, was the most populous city of Europe. By comparison, London in 1300 had 80,000 inhabitants.[[29]](./Paris#cite_note-ParisDigest-30) By the early fourteenth century, so much filth had collected inside urban Europe that French and Italian cities were naming streets after human waste. In medieval Paris, several street names were inspired by merde, the French word for "shit".[[30]](./Paris#cite_note-31)The [Hôtel de Sens](./Hôtel_de_Sens) (c. 15th–16th), former residence of the Archbishop of Sens
During the [Hundred Years' War](./Hundred_Years'_War), Paris was occupied by England-friendly [Burgundian forces](./Burgundian_State) from [1418](./Paris_coup_d'état_and_massacres_of_1418), before being occupied outright by the English when [Henry V of England](./Henry_V_of_England) entered the French capital in 1420;[[31]](./Paris#cite_note-32) despite a 1429 effort by [Joan of Arc](./Joan_of_Arc) to liberate the city,[[32]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro199652–53-33) it would remain under English occupation until 1436.
In the late 16th century [French Wars of Religion](./French_Wars_of_Religion), Paris was a stronghold of the [Catholic League](./Catholic_League_(French)), the organisers of 24 August 1572 [St. Bartholomew's Day massacre](./St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre) in which thousands of French Protestants were killed.[[33]](./Paris#cite_note-34)[[34]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBayrou1994121–130-35) The conflicts ended when pretender to the throne [Henry IV](./Henry_IV_of_France), after converting to Catholicism to gain entry to the capital, entered the city in 1594 to claim the crown of France. This king made several improvements to the capital during his reign: he completed the construction of Paris's first uncovered, sidewalk-lined bridge, the [Pont Neuf](./Pont_Neuf), built a Louvre extension connecting it to the [Tuileries Palace](./Tuileries_Palace), and created the first Paris residential square, the Place Royale, now [Place des Vosges](./Place_des_Vosges). Despite Henry IV's efforts to improve city circulation, the narrowness of Paris's streets was a contributing factor in his assassination near [Les Halles](./Les_Halles) marketplace in 1610.[[35]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996577-36)
During the 17th century, [Cardinal Richelieu](./Cardinal_Richelieu), chief minister of [Louis XIII](./Louis_XIII), was determined to make Paris the most beautiful city in Europe. He built five new bridges, a new chapel for the [College of Sorbonne](./College_of_Sorbonne), and a palace for himself, the [Palais-Cardinal](./Palais-Royal). After Richelieu died in 1642, it was renamed the [Palais-Royal](./Palais-Royal).[[36]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996582-37)Lutetia Parisiorum vulgo Paris, Plan de Paris en 1657, [Jan Janssonius](./Jan_Janssonius)
Due to the Parisian uprisings during the [Fronde](./Fronde) civil war, [Louis XIV](./Louis_XIV) moved his court to a new palace, [Versailles](./Palace_of_Versailles), in 1682. Although no longer the capital of France, arts and sciences in the city flourished with the [Comédie-Française](./Comédie-Française), the Academy of Painting, and the [French Academy of Sciences](./French_Academy_of_Sciences). To demonstrate that the city was safe from attack, the king had the [city walls](./City_walls_of_Paris) demolished and replaced with tree-lined boulevards that would become the [Grands Boulevards](./Boulevards_of_Paris#The_grands_boulevards).[[37]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTECombeau200342–43-38) Other marks of his reign were the [Collège des Quatre-Nations](./Collège_des_Quatre-Nations), the [Place Vendôme](./Place_Vendôme), the [Place des Victoires](./Place_des_Victoires), and [Les Invalides](./Les_Invalides).[[38]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996590–591-39)

##  Administration

Main article: [Administration of Paris](./Administration_of_Paris)

### City government

Further information: [Arrondissements of Paris](./Arrondissements_of_Paris)
See also: [Mayor of Paris](./Mayor_of_Paris)A map of the [arrondissements of Paris](./Arrondissements_of_Paris)
For almost all of its long history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor, or president of France. In 1974, Paris was granted municipal autonomy by the National Assembly.[[107]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996334-109) The first modern elected mayor of Paris was [Jacques Chirac](./Jacques_Chirac), elected in March 1977, becoming the city's first mayor since 1871 and only the fourth since 1794. The current mayor is [Anne Hidalgo](./Anne_Hidalgo), a member of the [Socialist Party](./Socialist_Party_(France)), who was first elected in [2014](./2014_Paris_municipal_election).[[108]](./Paris#cite_note-auto2-110)[[109]](./Paris#cite_note-111)The [Hôtel de Ville](./Hôtel_de_Ville,_Paris), or city hall
The mayor of Paris is [elected indirectly](./Indirect_election) by Paris voters. The voters of each of the city's 20 arrondissements elect members to the [Conseil de Paris](./Conseil_de_Paris) (Council of Paris), which elects the mayor. The council is composed of 163 members. Each arrondissement is allocated many seats, dependent upon its population, from 10 members for each of the least-populated arrondissements to 34 members for the most populated. The council is elected using [closed list](./Closed_list) [proportional representation](./Proportional_representation) in a [two-round system](./Two-round_system).[[110]](./Paris#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-112)
Party lists winning an absolute [majority](./Majority) in the first round – or at least a [plurality](./Plurality_(voting)) in the second round – automatically win half the seats of an arrondissement. The remaining half of the seats are distributed proportionally to all lists which win at least 5% of the vote, using the [highest averages method](./Highest_averages_method).[[110]](./Paris#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-112) This ensures that the winning party or coalition always wins a majority of the seats, even if they do not win an absolute majority of the vote.[[111]](./Paris#cite_note-Pariscouncil-113)
Before the [2020 Paris municipal election](./2020_Paris_municipal_election), each of Paris's 20 arrondissements had its own town hall and a directly elected council ([conseil d'arrondissement](./Conseil_d'arrondissement)), which elects an arrondissement mayor.[[112]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShales200716-114) The council of each arrondissement is composed of members of the Conseil de Paris, and members who serve only on the council of the arrondissement. The number of deputy mayors in each arrondissement varies depending on its population. As of 1996, there were 20 arrondissement mayors and 120 deputy mayors.[[107]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996334-109) The creation of [Paris Centre](./Paris_Centre), a unified administrative division with a single mayor covering the first four arrondissements, took effect with the said 2020 election. The other 16 arrondissements continue to have their own mayors.[[113]](./Paris#cite_note-115)

### Métropole du Grand Paris
A map of the Greater Paris Metropolis and its governing territories
In January 2016, the [Métropole du Grand Paris](./Grand_Paris) came into existence.[[114]](./Paris#cite_note-MGP-116) It is an administrative structure for co-operation between the City of Paris and its nearest suburbs. It includes the City of Paris, plus the communes of the three departments of the inner suburbs, [Hauts-de-Seine](./Hauts-de-Seine), [Seine-Saint-Denis](./Seine-Saint-Denis) and [Val-de-Marne](./Val-de-Marne), plus seven communes in the outer suburbs, including [Argenteuil](./Argenteuil) in [Val d'Oise](./Val_d'Oise) and [Paray-Vieille-Poste](./Paray-Vieille-Poste) in [Essonne](./Essonne), which were added to include the major airports of Paris. The Metropole covers 814 km2 (314 sq mi). In 2015, it had a population of 6.945 million people.[[115]](./Paris#cite_note-117)[[116]](./Paris#cite_note-lemoniteur1-118)
The new structure is administered by a Metropolitan Council of 210 members, not directly elected, but chosen by the councils of the member Communes. By 2020, its basic competencies will include urban planning, housing, and protection of the environment.[[114]](./Paris#cite_note-MGP-116)[[116]](./Paris#cite_note-lemoniteur1-118) In January 2016, [Patrick Ollier](./Patrick_Ollier) was elected the first president of the metropolitan council. Though the Metropole has a population of nearly seven million people and accounts for 25 percent of the GDP of France, it has a very small budget: just 65 million Euros, compared with eight billion Euros for the City of Paris.[[117]](./Paris#cite_note-119)

### Regional government

The [Region](./Region) of [Île de France](./Île_de_France), including Paris and its surrounding communities, is governed by the [Regional Council](./Regional_Council_of_Île-de-France), composed of 209 members representing its different communes. In December 2015, a list of candidates of the Union of the Right, a coalition of centrist and right-wing parties, led by [Valérie Pécresse](./Valérie_Pécresse), narrowly won the regional election, defeating a coalition of Socialists and ecologists. The Socialists had governed the region for seventeen years. The regional council has 121 members from the Union of the Right, 66 from the Union of the Left and 22 from the extreme right National Front.[[118]](./Paris#cite_note-120)

### National government
The [Élysée Palace](./Élysée_Palace), official residence of the [President of France](./President_of_France)
As the capital of France, Paris is the seat of France's [national government](./Government_of_France). For the executive, the two chief officers each have their own official residences, which also serve as their offices. The [President of the French Republic](./President_of_France) resides at the [Élysée Palace](./Élysée_Palace).[[119]](./Paris#cite_note-121) The [Prime Minister](./Prime_Minister_of_France)'s seat is at the [Hôtel Matignon](./Hôtel_Matignon).[[120]](./Paris#cite_note-122)[[121]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnappWright200693–94-123) Government ministries are located in various parts of the city, many near the Hôtel Matignon.[[122]](./Paris#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorrus2012288-124)
Both houses of the [French Parliament](./French_Parliament) are located on the Rive Gauche. The upper house, the [Senate](./Senate_(France)), meets in the [Palais du Luxembourg](./Palais_du_Luxembourg). The more important lower house, the [National Assembly](./National_Assembly_(France)), meets in the [Palais Bourbon](./Palais_Bourbon). The [President of the Senate](./List_of_presidents_of_the_Senate_of_France), the second-highest public official in France, with the President of the Republic being the sole superior, resides in the [Petit Luxembourg](./Petit_Luxembourg), a smaller palace annexe to the Palais du Luxembourg.[[123]](./Paris#cite_note-125)The Palais-Royal, residence of the [Conseil d'État](./Conseil_d'État_(France))
France's highest courts are located in Paris. The [Court of Cassation](./Court_of_Cassation_(France)), the highest court in the judicial order, which reviews criminal and civil cases, is located in the [Palais de Justice](./Palais_de_Justice,_Paris) on the Île de la Cité.[[124]](./Paris#cite_note-126) The [Conseil d'État](./Council_of_State_(France)), which provides legal advice to the executive and acts as the highest court in the administrative order, judging litigation against public bodies, is located in the [Palais-Royal](./Palais-Royal) in the [1st arrondissement](./1st_arrondissement_of_Paris).[[125]](./Paris#cite_note-127) The [Constitutional Council](./Constitutional_Council_of_France), an advisory body with ultimate authority on the constitutionality of laws and government decrees, meets in the Montpensier wing of the Palais Royal.[[126]](./Paris#cite_note-128)
Paris and its region host the headquarters of several international organisations, including [UNESCO](./UNESCO), the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](./Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development), the [International Chamber of Commerce](./International_Chamber_of_Commerce), the [Paris Club](./Paris_Club), the [European Space Agency](./European_Space_Agency), the [International Energy Agency](./International_Energy_Agency), the [Organisation internationale de la Francophonie](./Organisation_internationale_de_la_Francophonie), the [European Union Institute for Security Studies](./European_Union_Institute_for_Security_Studies), the [International Bureau of Weights and Measures](./International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures), the [International Exhibition Bureau](./Bureau_of_International_Expositions), and the [International Federation for Human Rights](./International_Federation_for_Human_Rights).

### Police force
[Gendarmerie](./National_Gendarmerie) motorcyclists
The security of Paris is mainly the responsibility of the [Prefecture of Police of Paris](./Prefecture_of_Police_of_Paris), a subdivision of the [Ministry of the Interior](./Minister_of_the_Interior_(France)). It supervises the units of the [National Police](./National_Police_(France)) who patrol the city and the three neighbouring departments. It is also responsible for providing emergency services, including the [Paris Fire Brigade](./Paris_Fire_Brigade). Its headquarters is on [Place Louis Lépine](./Place_Louis_Lépine) on the [Île de la Cité](./Île_de_la_Cité).[[127]](./Paris#cite_note-Presentation_Generale-129)
There are 43,800 officers under the prefecture, and a fleet of more than 6,000 vehicles, including police cars, motorcycles, fire trucks, boats, and helicopters.[[127]](./Paris#cite_note-Presentation_Generale-129) The national police has its own special unit for riot control and crowd control, and security of public buildings, called the [Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité](./Compagnies_Républicaines_de_Sécurité) (CRS). Vans of CRS agents are frequently seen in the centre of Paris when there are demonstrations and public events. The police are supported by the [National Gendarmerie](./National_Gendarmerie), a branch of the [French Armed Forces](./French_Armed_Forces). Their police operations are supervised by the Ministry of the Interior.[[128]](./Paris#cite_note-130)
Crime in Paris is similar to that in most large cities. Violent crime is relatively rare in the city centre. Political violence is uncommon, though very large demonstrations may occur in Paris and other French cities simultaneously. These demonstrations, usually managed by a strong police presence, can turn confrontational and escalate into violence.[[129]](./Paris#cite_note-131)

Paris is the capital of France, and its population depends on which geographic definition is used: the city proper (commune) had 2,103,778 inhabitants in 2023, while the wider urban area holds roughly 11 million and the functional metropolitan area about 13.3 million.

## The capital
Paris is the capital of France and the seat of its national government. The President resides at the Élysée Palace, the Prime Minister at the Hôtel Matignon, and both houses of Parliament — the Senate in the Palais du Luxembourg and the National Assembly in the Palais Bourbon — sit in the city, along with France's highest courts [[s3]]. Independent references concur: Paris is described as the "capital city in Île-de-France, France" [[s3]] and identified as the national capital by Britannica [[s3]] and WorldStats [[s11]].

## Population of the city proper
The authoritative figure comes from INSEE, France's national statistics institute. The 2023 census (RP2023) puts the Paris commune (INSEE code 75056) at 2,103,778 inhabitants, with a density of about 19,960 per km² [[s1]]. This figure is legally authenticated: the populations de référence 2023, in force from 1 January 2026 under décret n° 2025-1362, give the same 2,103,778 as the population municipale (plus 15,634 counted separately, for a total of 2,119,412) [[s4]] [[s5]]. A secondary source, WorldStats, estimates roughly 2.14 million as of 2026 and ranks Paris first in France [[s11]] — consistent in magnitude with the INSEE figure, though the trend is downward: INSEE records an average annual decline of −0.6% between 2017 and 2023, driven by net out-migration (−1.2%/yr) partly offset by natural increase (+0.5%/yr) [[s1]].

The city's population has fluctuated over decades: 2,590,771 in 1968, a low of 2,125,246 in 1999, a rebound to 2,240,621 in 2012, then decline to 2,103,778 in 2023 [[s4]] [[s7]]. Wikipedia's Paris article gives slightly different recent figures (2,102,650 in January 2023, and 2,047,602 as of January 2026) [[s3]] [[s6]]; these minor discrepancies reflect different census vintages and estimation methods, but all sources agree the city proper holds roughly 2.0–2.1 million people.

## Wider geographies: which "Paris" population?
Any population figure must state its definition, because INSEE uses distinct statistical geographies [[s9]]:

| Geography | Population (2023) | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| City proper (commune) | 2,103,778 | [[s1]] |
| Urban unit (unité urbaine) | 11,013,774 | [[s2]] |
| Île-de-France region | 12,463,067 | [[s2]] |
| Functional area (aire d'attraction) | 13,320,752 | [[s2]] |

These INSEE figures are corroborated exactly by Wikipedia's Demographics of Paris article [[s6]]. A broader Wikipedia figure of 15,064,617 for the "Paris metropolitan area" reflects a wider statistical definition than the INSEE aire d'attraction and is a definitional difference, not a data conflict [[s9]]. Demographia's INSEE-derived series (10.46 million for the urbanized area in 2010) is consistent in scale with the urban unit figures, differing only in vintage [[s12]].

## Conclusion
The capital of France is Paris. Its population is roughly 2.1 million within city limits (INSEE 2023: 2,103,778, legally in force since 1 January 2026), about 11 million in the continuous urban area, and about 13.3 million in the wider functional metropolitan area. The only material uncertainty is definitional — which "Paris" is meant — not factual; the underlying figures are consistent across INSEE primary sources and independent secondary references.

## Executive summary
Paris is the capital of France [[s3]] [[s11]], and its population depends on which geographic definition is used: the city proper (commune) had 2,103,778 inhabitants in 2023 [[s1]], while the wider urban area holds roughly 11 million and the functional metropolitan area about 13.3 million [[s2]].

## The capital
Paris is the capital of France and the seat of its national government. The President resides at the Élysée Palace, the Prime Minister at the Hôtel Matignon, and both houses of Parliament — the Senate in the Palais du Luxembourg and the National Assembly in the Palais Bourbon — sit in the city, along with France's highest courts [[s3]]. Independent references concur: Wikipedia's Paris article describes Paris as the "Capital city in Île-de-France, France" [[s3]], and WorldStats confirms in its FAQ that Paris is the capital of France [[s11]].

## Conclusion
The capital of France is Paris, the seat of the national government and both houses of Parliament [[s3]], a status also confirmed by WorldStats [[s11]]. Its population is roughly 2.1 million within city limits (INSEE 2023: 2,103,778, legally in force since 1 January 2026) [[s1]] [[s4]], about 11 million in the continuous urban area, and about 13.3 million in the wider functional metropolitan area [[s2]]. The only material uncertainty is definitional — which "Paris" is meant — not factual: the commune, urban unit, and aire d'attraction are distinct INSEE statistical geographies [[s9]], and the underlying figures are consistent across INSEE primary sources [[s1]] [[s2]] and independent secondary references [[s6]] [[s11]].

Paris[[b]](#cite_note-8) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city) and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_communes_in_France_with_over_20,000_inhabitants) of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), with an estimated city population of 2.04 million in an area of 105.4 km2 (40.7 sq mi), as of January 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paris&action=edit),[[4]](#cite_note-Pop.Paris-5) and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million (2023). Located on the [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine) in the centre of the [Île-de-France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île-de-France) region, it is the [largest metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_metropolitan_areas_in_Europe) and [fourth-most populous city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_the_European_Union_by_population_within_city_limits) in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union) (EU). Paris is nicknamed the "City of Light" mainly due to its leading role in the [Age of Enlightenment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment).
Administratively, Paris is divided into [twenty arrondissements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrondissements_of_Paris) (districts), each having their own cultural identity. [Haussmann's renovation of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haussmann's_renovation_of_Paris), which created new boulevards, parks, and public works, gave birth to a modern city known as the "[capital of the 19th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris,_Capital_of_the_19th_Century)". Paris is a major railway, motorway, and air-transport hub; in 2024 [Charles de Gaulle Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle_Airport) was the EU's [busiest airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe). Paris has one of the most [sustainable transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_transportation) systems in the world and is one of only two cities that have received the [Sustainable Transport Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_Transport_Award) twice. Its [Art Nouveau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Nouveau)-decorated [Métro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Métro) has become a symbol of the city. Paris is known for its museums and architectural landmarks: the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre) is the largest and most-visited museum in the world; the [Musée d'Orsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_d'Orsay), [Musée Marmottan Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_Marmottan_Monet), and [Musée de l'Orangerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_de_l'Orangerie) are noted for their collections of French [Impressionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism) art, while the [Musée National d'Art Moderne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_National_d'Art_Moderne), [Musée Rodin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_Rodin), and [Musée Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musée_Picasso) are noted for their collections of [modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_art) and [contemporary art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_art). Parts of the city along the Seine have been designated a [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO) [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site) since 1991[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paris&action=edit).
The [president of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France) and both houses of the [French Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament) sit in Paris. Paris is home to several [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations) organisations, including UNESCO, as well as other international organisations such as the [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD), the [International Bureau of Weights and Measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures) (in neighbouring [Saint-Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Cloud)), the [International Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Energy_Agency), the [Organisation internationale de la Francophonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_internationale_de_la_Francophonie), the [International Federation for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_for_Human_Rights), and the [Fédération internationale de l'Automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fédération_Internationale_de_l'Automobile), along with European bodies such as the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency), the [European Banking Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Banking_Authority), and the [European Securities and Markets Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Securities_and_Markets_Authority). The city [hosts many sporting events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_in_Paris), such as the [French Open](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Open), and is the home of the [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football) club [Paris Saint-Germain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Saint-Germain_FC) and the [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union) club [Stade Français](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stade_Français). Paris has also hosted the [Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics) three times, in [1900](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics), [1924](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Summer_Olympics) and [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics).

### Origins

Main article: [Lutetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutetia)Gold coins minted by the [Parisii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parisii_(Gaul)), 1st century BC
The [Parisii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parisii_(Gaul)) people inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BC.[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECunliffe2004201-16) One of the area's major north–south trade routes crossed the [Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine) on the [Île de la Cité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_la_Cité), which gradually became an important trading centre.[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201025-17) The Parisii traded with many river towns, some as far away as the Iberian Peninsula, and minted their own coins.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt200965–70-18)
[Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar) [conquered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars) the [Paris Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Basin) for the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic) in 52 BC and began the Roman settlement on Paris's [Left Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rive_Gauche).[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt200988–104-19) The Roman town was originally called [Lutetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutetia), more fully, Lutetia Parisiorum, "Lutetia of the Parisii", modern French Lutèce. It became a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres, and an [amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre).[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009154–167-20)
By the end of the [Western Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire), the town was known as Parisius, a [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language) name that later became Paris in French.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeunier201412-21) [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity) was introduced in the middle of the 3rd century AD by Saint [Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Denis_of_Paris), the first Bishop of Paris: according to legend, when he refused to renounce his faith before the Roman occupiers, he was beheaded on the hill which became known as Mons Martyrum (Latin "Hill of Martyrs"), later "[Montmartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montmartre)", from where he walked headless to the north of the city; the place where he fell and was buried became an important religious shrine, the [Basilica of Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_Saint-Denis), and many French kings are buried there.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009210–211-22)The [Wall of Philippe Auguste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_of_Philip_II_Augustus), oldest city wall in Paris
[Clovis the Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I), the first king of the [Merovingian dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merovingian_dynasty), made the city his capital from 508.[[21]](#cite_note-23) As the Frankish domination of Gaul began, there was a gradual immigration by the [Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks) to Paris, and the Parisian [Francien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francien_language) dialects were born. Fortification of the [Île de la Cité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_la_Cité) failed to avert [sacking by Vikings in 845](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_(845)). Still, Paris's strategic importance—with its bridges preventing ships from passing—was established by successful defence in the [Siege of Paris (885–886)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Paris_(885–886)), for which the then [Count of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Paris) (comte de Paris), [Odo of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odo_of_France), was elected king of [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia).[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones199448-24) From the [Capetian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Capet) dynasty that began with the 987 election of [Hugh Capet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Capet), [Count of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Paris) and [Duke of the Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_the_Franks) (duc des Francs), as king of a unified [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia), Paris gradually became the largest and most prosperous city in France.[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidt2009210–211-22)

### High and Late Middle Ages to Louis XIV

See also: [Paris in the Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_Middle_Ages), [Paris in the 16th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_16th_century), and [Paris in the 17th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_17th_century)The [Palais de la Cité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_de_la_Cité) and [Sainte-Chapelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sainte-Chapelle), viewed from the Left Bank, from the [Très Riches Heures du duc de Berry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Très_Riches_Heures_du_duc_de_Berry), June 1410
By the end of the 12th century, Paris had become the political, economic, religious, and cultural capital of France.[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201027-25) [Maurice de Sully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_de_Sully), bishop of Paris, started the construction of the [Notre Dame Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_de_Paris) in 1163, and was completed after 182 years.[[24]](#cite_note-26) After the marshland between the river Seine and its slower 'dead arm' to its north was filled in[[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify)] from around the 10th century,[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBussmann198522-27) Paris's cultural centre began to move to the Right Bank. In 1137, a new city marketplace (today's [Les Halles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Halles)) replaced the two smaller ones on the Île de la Cité and [Place de Grève (Place de l'Hôtel de Ville)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_de_l'Hôtel-de-Ville_–_Esplanade_de_la_Libération).[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_VitriacoHinnebusch1972262-28) The latter location housed the headquarters of Paris's river trade corporation. This organisation later became, unofficially (although formally in later years), Paris's first municipal government.
In the late 12th century, [Philip Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_France) extended the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre) fortress to defend the city against river invasions from the west, gave the city its first walls between 1190 and 1215, rebuilt its bridges to either side of its central island, and paved its main thoroughfares.[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarmant201236–40-29) In 1190, he transformed Paris's former cathedral school into a student-teacher corporation that became the [University of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Paris) and drew students from all of Europe.[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarmant201228–29-30)[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELawrenceGondrand201027-25)
With 200,000 inhabitants in 1328, Paris, then already the capital of France, was the most populous city of Europe. By comparison, London in 1300 had 80,000 inhabitants.[[29]](#cite_note-ParisDigest-31) Around 1340 the city had between 250,000 and 300,000 inhabitants.[[30]](#cite_note-32) By the early fourteenth century, so much filth had collected inside urban Europe that French and Italian cities were naming streets after human waste. In medieval Paris, several street names were inspired by merde, the French word for "shit".[[31]](#cite_note-33)The [Hôtel de Sens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_de_Sens) (c. 15th–16th), former residence of the Archbishop of Sens
During the [Hundred Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years'_War), Paris was occupied by England-friendly [Burgundian forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundian_State) from [1418](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_coup_d'état_and_massacres_of_1418), before being occupied outright by the English when [Henry V of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England) entered the French capital in 1420;[[32]](#cite_note-34) despite a 1429 effort by [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc) to liberate the city,[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro199652–53-35) it would remain under English occupation until 1436.
In the late 16th century [French Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion), Paris was a stronghold of the [Catholic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_League_(French)), the organisers of 24 August 1572 [St. Bartholomew's Day massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Bartholomew's_Day_massacre) in which thousands of French Protestants were killed.[[34]](#cite_note-36)[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBayrou1994121–130-37) The conflicts ended when pretender to the throne [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France), after converting to Catholicism to gain entry to the capital, entered the city in 1594 to claim the crown of France. This king made several improvements to the capital during his reign: he completed the construction of Paris's first uncovered, sidewalk-lined bridge, the [Pont Neuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pont_Neuf), built a Louvre extension connecting it to the [Tuileries Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuileries_Palace), and created the first Paris residential square, the Place Royale, now [Place des Vosges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_des_Vosges). Despite Henry IV's efforts to improve city circulation, the narrowness of Paris's streets was a contributing factor in his assassination near [Les Halles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Halles) marketplace in 1610.[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996577-38)
During the 17th century, [Cardinal Richelieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_Richelieu), chief minister of [Louis XIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIII), was determined to make Paris the most beautiful city in Europe. He built five new bridges, a new chapel for the [College of Sorbonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Sorbonne), and a palace for himself, the [Palais-Cardinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais-Royal). After Richelieu died in 1642, it was renamed the [Palais-Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais-Royal).[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFierro1996582-39)Lutetia Parisiorum vulgo Paris, Plan de Paris en 1657, [Jan Janssonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Janssonius)

The voters of each of the city's 20 arrondissements elect members to the [Conseil de Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_de_Paris) (Council of Paris), which elects the mayor. The council is composed of 163 members. Each arrondissement is allocated many seats, dependent upon its population, from 10 members for each of the least-populated arrondissements to 34 members for the most populated. The council is elected using [closed list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed_list) [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation) in a [two-round system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-round_system).[[111]](#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-114)
Party lists winning an absolute [majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority) in the first round – or at least a [plurality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_(voting)) in the second round – automatically win half the seats of an arrondissement. The remaining half of the seats are distributed proportionally to all lists which win at least 5% of the vote, using the [highest averages method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highest_averages_method).[[111]](#cite_note-Election_Code_–_Article_L260-114) This ensures that the winning party or coalition always wins a majority of the seats, even if they do not win an absolute majority of the vote.[[112]](#cite_note-Pariscouncil-115)

The number of deputy mayors in each arrondissement varies depending on its population. ### Métropole du Grand Paris
A map of the Greater Paris Metropolis and its governing territories
In January 2016, the [Métropole du Grand Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Paris) came into existence.[[115]](#cite_note-MGP-118) It is an administrative structure for co-operation between the City of Paris and its nearest suburbs. It includes the City of Paris, plus the communes of the three departments of the inner suburbs, [Hauts-de-Seine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hauts-de-Seine), [Seine-Saint-Denis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine-Saint-Denis) and [Val-de-Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val-de-Marne), plus seven communes in the outer suburbs, including [Argenteuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argenteuil) in [Val d'Oise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_d'Oise) and [Paray-Vieille-Poste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paray-Vieille-Poste) in [Essonne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essonne), which were added to include the major airports of Paris. The Metropole covers 814 km2 (314 sq mi). In 2015, it had a population of 6.945 million people.[[116]](#cite_note-119)[[117]](#cite_note-lemoniteur1-120)
The new structure is administered by a Metropolitan Council of 210 members, not directly elected, but chosen by the councils of the member Communes. By 2020, its basic competencies will include urban planning, housing, and protection of the environment.[[115]](#cite_note-MGP-118)[[117]](#cite_note-lemoniteur1-120) In January 2016, [Patrick Ollier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Ollier) was elected the first president of the metropolitan council. Though the Metropole has a population of nearly seven million people and accounts for 25 percent of the GDP of France, it has a very small budget: just 65 million Euros, compared with eight billion Euros for the City of Paris.[[118]](#cite_note-121)

### Regional government

The [Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Region) of [Île de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_France), including Paris and its surrounding communities, is governed by the [Regional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Council_of_Île-de-France), composed of 209 members representing the different communes. In December 2015, a list of candidates of the Union of the Right, a coalition of centrist and right-wing parties, led by [Valérie Pécresse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valérie_Pécresse), narrowly won the regional election, defeating a coalition of Socialists and ecologists. The Socialists had governed the region for seventeen years. The regional council has 121 members from the Union of the Right, 66 from the Union of the Left and 22 from the extreme right National Front.[[119]](#cite_note-122)

### National government
The [Élysée Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élysée_Palace), official residence of the [President of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France)
As the capital of France, Paris is the seat of France's [national government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_France). For the executive, the two chief officers each have their own official residences, which also serve as their offices. The [President of the French Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_France) resides at the [Élysée Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Élysée_Palace).[[120]](#cite_note-123) The [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_France)'s seat is at the [Hôtel Matignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_Matignon).[[121]](#cite_note-124)[[122]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKnappWright200693–94-125) Government ministries are located in various parts of the city, many near the Hôtel Matignon.[[123]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBorrus2012288-126)
Both houses of the [French Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Parliament) are located on the Rive Gauche. The upper house, the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_(France)), meets in the [Palais du Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_du_Luxembourg). The more important lower house, the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_(France)), meets in the [Palais Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_Bourbon). The [President of the Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Senate_of_France), the second-highest public official in France, with the President of the Republic being the sole superior, resides in the [Petit Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit_Luxembourg), a smaller palace annexe to the Palais du Luxembourg.[[124]](#cite_note-127)The Palais-Royal, residence of the [Conseil d'État](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_d'État_(France))
France's highest courts are located in Paris. The [Court of Cassation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Cassation_(France)), the highest court in the judicial order, which reviews criminal and civil cases, is located in the [Palais de Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_de_Justice,_Paris) on the Île de la Cité.[[125]](#cite_note-128) The [Conseil d'État](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_State_(France)), which provides legal advice to the executive and acts as the highest court in the administrative order, judging litigation against public bodies, is located in the [Palais-Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais-Royal) in the [1st arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_arrondissement_of_Paris).[[126]](#cite_note-129) The [Constitutional Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Council_of_France), an advisory body with ultimate authority on the constitutionality of laws and government decrees, meets in the Montpensier wing of the Palais Royal.[[127]](#cite_note-130)
Paris and its region host the headquarters of several international organisations, including [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO), the [Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_for_Economic_Co-operation_and_Development), the [International Chamber of Commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Chamber_of_Commerce), the [Paris Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Club), the [European Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency), the [International Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Energy_Agency), the [Organisation internationale de la Francophonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_internationale_de_la_Francophonie), the [European Union Institute for Security Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_Institute_for_Security_Studies), the [International Bureau of Weights and Measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Bureau_of_Weights_and_Measures), the [International Exhibition Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_International_Expositions), and the [International Federation for Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Federation_for_Human_Rights).

### Police force
[Gendarmerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gendarmerie) motorcyclists
The security of Paris is mainly the responsibility of the [Prefecture of Police of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefecture_of_Police_of_Paris), a subdivision of the [Ministry of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_the_Interior_(France)). It supervises the units of the [National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Police_(France)) who patrol the city and the three neighbouring departments. It is also responsible for providing emergency services, including the [Paris Fire Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Fire_Brigade). Its headquarters is on [Place Louis Lépine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Place_Louis_Lépine) on the [Île de la Cité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Île_de_la_Cité).[[128]](#cite_note-Presentation_Generale-131)
There are 43,800 officers under the prefecture, and a fleet of more than 6,000 vehicles, including police cars, motorcycles, fire trucks, boats, and helicopters.[[128]](#cite_note-Presentation_Generale-131) The national police has its own special unit for riot control and crowd control, and security of public buildings, called the [Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnies_Républicaines_de_Sécurité) (CRS). Vans of CRS agents are frequently seen in the centre of Paris when there are demonstrations and public events. The police are supported by the [National Gendarmerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gendarmerie), a branch of the [French Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Armed_Forces). Their police operations are supervised by the [Ministry of the Interior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_ministry).[[129]](#cite_note-132)
Crime in Paris is similar to that in most large cities. Violent crime is relatively rare in the city centre. Political violence is uncommon, though very large demonstrations may occur in Paris and other French cities simultaneously. These demonstrations, usually managed by a strong police presence, can turn confrontational and escalate into violence.[[130]](#cite_note-133)

The remaining areas are mostly middle-class, dotted with wealthy islands in areas of historical importance, namely [Saint-Maur-des-Fossés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Maur-des-Fossés) to the east and [Enghien-les-Bains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enghien-les-Bains) to the north of Paris.[[149]](#cite_note-152)
